Connecting the DotsThere’s a world behind a dot.

Why does a Caribbean island have a name associated with artificial intelligence? Who can give a city its own place on the Internet? Discover the stories, money and identities behind .com, .ai and other Internet names.

A FIRST LOOKFour everyday situations behind a dotA shop, an AI service, a language, your city. No technical knowledge needed.Guided reading · about 3 minutes →

The end of an address looks like a small detail. Yet it can speak of businesses, territories and communities. These situations are illustrative; the names and facts lead to documented cases. Reading time is an estimate: pause wherever you like.

  1. 01example.com

    You take a small business online

    The name above the door is not the shop.

    Imagine putting your shop’s catalogue online. In example.com, .com is the final extension, called a TLD. Registering a name and building a website are different tasks: having an address does not mean you already have pages, products or customers. Likewise, a ranking of registered domains is not a ranking of visited websites. example.com is reserved for examples; it is not a real business.

    When you see a number, ask what it counts: addresses, websites or visits?

    Compare the two rankings →
    Sources and context
    • IANA · Example domains
    • RFC 1034 · Domain names: concepts and facilities
  2. 02.ai

    You come across a new AI service

    Two technological letters, a Caribbean history.

    You see .ai and think of artificial intelligence. But .ai is the country code for Anguilla, in the Caribbean. A name can keep its function while acquiring a new association. For someone choosing an address, it is also a way to present themselves; for a reader, it is a clue to interpret. The suffix alone establishes neither where the service is located nor the quality of what it offers.

    The association you recognise in a name does not tell its whole history.

    Follow the story of .ai →
    Sources and context
    • IANA · .ai / Anguilla
  3. 03.cat

    You look for a place for your language

    Belonging can cross state borders.

    Imagine an association that wants to be recognised through the language it uses. .cat was created for the Catalan linguistic and cultural community: the 2005 IANA report documents this purpose. Here a name represents a community rather than a country code. For a publisher, choosing a name can also express belonging. That alone does not measure how many people feel included or use those websites.

    Names can express identity; their effects on people require observation.

    Explore the case and its sources →
    Sources and context
    • IANA · .CAT delegation report (2005)
  4. 04.lugano

    Your city proposes its own extension

    Applying for a name does not mean it has been granted.

    You wonder whether city services will have a new address. In the 2026 corpus documented here, .lugano is an application, not an operational extension. Submitting an application guarantees neither approval nor public availability. Decisions about who could use the name and for which services remain to be established. As a citizen, you can ask which uses are proposed, what resources they need and how their results would be assessed.

    Always distinguish a proposal, a decision and an available service.

    Check its status and open decisions →

Application status refers to the sources and dates shown in the case records, not to a real-time check.

Three ideas to take with you

Try explaining them to someone in your own words; then compare them here.

Revisit the three distinctions
  • An address is not a website, and neither is a count of visits.
  • A name can express an activity, a territory or a community; its meaning can change.
  • An application is not an approval: status, date and source are part of the story.

START HERE · NO TECHNICAL KNOWLEDGE NEEDED

Behind a click: how the Internet works

When you open a website, its name helps find the computer that responds. Follow the steps one at a time.

What you typedhttps://www.example.com./news
What the Internet is doing now
https://www.example.com/news→the browser separates the URL into parts

How to communicate · which name to find · which resource to request.

READ THE ADDRESSStep 1 of 7

A URL tells the browser how, where and what to ask for

You typed https://www.example.com/news. https:// says how to communicate; www.example.com is the name to reach; /news is the requested resource. Before anything travels, the browser separates those jobs.

REMEMBER THISA URL is not just a website name: it contains different instructions for the browser.
One level deeper

A URL can also contain a port, query parameters and a fragment. We use a deliberately simple address here so the roles are visible without extra syntax.

The browser has to find www.example.com

People use readable names; the network needs to know which IP address should receive the data. The browser therefore relies on a DNS resolver to find where www.example.com can be reached.

REMEMBER THISNames are for people; IP addresses let networks reach destinations.
One level deeper

If a valid answer is already cached on the device or resolver, much of the DNS lookup can be skipped. The resolver may be supplied by your provider, organization or a service you choose.

DNS follows a hierarchy

If the answer is not already cached, the resolver can start at the DNS root. The root points to .com; the .com servers point to the DNS responsible for example.com. The final dot in www.example.com. represents the root and is normally omitted.

REMEMBER THIS.com is not decoration: it is a real level in the DNS hierarchy.
One level deeper

The root and TLD mostly provide delegations: directions about where to ask next. They do not host the web page or carry its content. Running a TLD is a different role from hosting a website.

The name becomes an IP address

The authoritative DNS for example.com returns the requested data. The resolver gives it to your device. In this simulation: www.example.com → 192.0.2.10.

REMEMBER THISDNS does not carry the page: it turns a name into information that helps locate the service.
One level deeper

Authoritative DNS servers publish data for the domains they serve. A records contain IPv4 addresses; AAAA records contain IPv6 addresses. One name can have several addresses, and several names can share an address.

Now the network knows where to send the packets

With the IP address available, packets can cross routers and networks until they reach the server. The Internet is not one network: it is a network of networks exchanging traffic.

REMEMBER THISThe IP identifies the destination; routers decide hop by hop how to reach it.
One level deeper

IP handles addressing and forwarding without guaranteeing delivery on its own. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 normally use TCP; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP. These transport choices sit above IP and help the exchange arrive reliably and efficiently.

The browser creates a protected connection

For HTTPS, the browser checks the certificate presented by the server for the requested name and establishes an encrypted connection. Data can now travel protected between browser and server.

REMEMBER THISHTTPS protects the transport and authenticates the server for that name; it does not guarantee that the content is true or trustworthy.
One level deeper

HTTPS protects communication and authenticates the server for that name. It does not certify that the operator is honest or the content is true. DNSSEC has a different job: verifying the origin and integrity of DNS data.

The browser asks for /news and builds what you see

Over the ready connection, the browser requests /news. The server responds with content and instructions; the browser interprets HTML, CSS, images and JavaScript and assembles the page.

REMEMBER THISThe page is the response to a request: the domain is the name used to reach the service, not the page itself.
One level deeper

A visit may require more files, other servers and additional DNS lookups. A domain name and a website are separate things: you can move the content while keeping the same name and changing DNS.

An URL gives the browser three instructions

HOWhttps://Use the Web over a protected connection
WHEREwww.example.comFind this name and the server behind it
WHAT/newsRequest this resource

An example page
RECAP

From the URL to the page, at a glance

These are conceptual stages, not a stopwatch: caches and existing connections can skip or overlap some of them. The chain is what matters.

  1. 1URLhttps://www.example.com/news
  2. 2Namewww.example.com
  3. 3DNS. → .com → example.com
  4. 4IP192.0.2.10
  5. 5Networkrouter → server
  6. 6HTTPSTLS
  7. 7PageGET /news → HTML

The whole path: URL → name → DNS → IP → networks → HTTPS → request → page.

An educational simulation, with no requests to the example website. 192.0.2.10 is reserved for documentation; it is not the real address of example.com.

This journey is simplified: caches and existing connections can skip some steps; others can overlap. A nearby server holding a copy may also deliver the page.

What does this archive count?
The locally archived 2000/2004/2012 applicant–string archive contains 1,987 records (2000, 2004, 2012). The Explorer has 2,788 browsable TLD/string records including 980 proposed 2026 strings from a secondary index. Separately, the new official ICANN APS CSV lists 2,783 rows for 1,614 public applications plus 1,169 replacement records. One of ICANN's 1,615 total (.wdo) lacks a public listing. Coverage and limits

This is a dated root/IANA snapshot, not a live feed. The 2000, 2004 and 2012 application corpora are complete locally at applied-for-string/applicant level. The 2012 layer covers all 1,930 applications, all 1,409 distinct Reveal-Day strings and all four ICANN-approved post-Reveal string corrections, producing 1,412 application-string lifecycle labels in total. Richer fields from the original 14-column 2012 transport are not all republished, and personal contact/email fields are excluded by design. For 2026, the public ICANN APS Applications CSV is locally archived with 2,783 rows for 1,614 published application IDs (including 1,169 replacement-string records), against 1,615 official applications; .wdo awaits administrative publication. The frozen 980-string secondary inventory used by the Explorer matches exactly the primary-string set derived from the APS listing after excluding the six applications for variants of existing TLDs. Complete individual application questionnaires and PDFs are not locally archived. Selection of replacement strings remains pending String Confirmation, while contention labels are not authoritative until String Evaluation. Alternative roots and special-use names are outside this catalogue. The 1,409 figure is the distinct-string count in the original 13 June 2012 Reveal-Day list. Later ICANN materials sometimes use 1,388 for later active/program-state populations; those figures are not the same snapshot.

The archaeology of the dot

Follow what was imagined, what was formally applied for, what reached the root, and how names later moved, changed operator, were retired or became disputed.
1984
PROTOCOL
Before .com, there was .arpaRFC 920 described .arpa as the initial, transitional top-level domain for the ARPA-Internet while the DNS was being introduced. It was supposed to disappear; instead it survived and today serves Internet infrastructure.
Source 1 ↗Source 2 ↗
1985
ROOT MILESTONE
The first .com: symbolics.comIn January 1985, .com, .edu, .gov, .mil, .net and .org joined .arpa in the root. On 15 March, symbolics.com became the first registered .com domain.
Source 1 ↗Source 2 ↗
1999
IDEA
The city idea appearsThe .berlin concept is traced back to 1999.
Source ↗
2000
APPLICATION ROUND
Proof of concept47 applications. Even .nyc appears, then withdraws.
Source ↗
2004
APPLICATION ROUND
Sponsored communities10 applications for 9 strings: .asia, .cat, .jobs, .mail, .mobi, .post, .tel, .travel and .xxx.
Source ↗
2012
APPLICATION ROUND
The explosion1,930 applications for 1,409 distinct strings, including 66 geographic applications.
Source ↗
2014
DELEGATION / LAUNCH
Cities go live.berlin opens to the public; .nyc and .paris are delegated.
Source ↗
2026
APPLICATION ROUND
The next layer1,615 applications are active at Reveal Day. ICANN has now published the applying entities and strings, including the official .lugano record.

Names, society and access

The names through which the Internet tells society's story

READING

Changing names, a changing network

A historical reading through documented cases. These changes overlap: older names live on and can acquire new meanings.

  1. 1984–1985

    Organising the network

    .com · .edu · .org

    Names distinguish functions and institutions.

    Case and sources →
  2. 1993–1994

    Being present

    .com

    With the Web, a name also becomes a storefront and service.

    Case and sources →
  3. 2000–2004

    Belonging

    .coop · .cat · .mobi

    Communities, languages and ways of connecting seek a space.

    Case and sources →
  4. 2010

    Using your own script

    مصر. · السعودية.

    The first Arabic-script country codes enter the DNS root.

    Case and sources →
  5. 2012 →

    Making a place

    .berlin · .google · .bank · .blog

    Cities, brands, access rules and publishing coexist.

    Case and sources →
  6. Today

    Reinterpreting names

    .ai

    An existing country code acquires a new cultural association.

    Case and sources →

These cases document particular histories. Name classification remains exploratory and cannot by itself measure society-wide change.

Reading method and limits

This is exploratory classification; independent validation has not been completed. Applied-for words document proposals, not by themselves a change in society as a whole. Comparing eras requires consistent rules, label review and evidence about actual use.

Beyond the dot lie institutions, markets, communities and ideas about the future. Reading TLDs over time helps us follow changes in the Internet and the ways people seek a place within it. This historical interpretation draws on documented cases: categories overlap, and existing names can acquire new meanings.

1984–1985 · defining the original categories

Before the Web: giving the network an order

Documented fact. In October 1984, RFC 920 describes .com for commercial activities, .edu for education, .gov for government, .mil for the military and .org for other organizations, alongside country codes. The Web would only be proposed in 1989: .com predates company websites.

Interpretation. The earliest naming map mainly reflects the institutions and administrative responsibilities of a network that predates the Web. Country codes place geography alongside this classification by function.

IETF · RFC 920, Domain Requirements (1984) ↗CERN · The birth of the Web ↗

1993–1994 · opening the Web and the growth of .com

An address becomes a public presence

Documented fact. On 30 April 1993, CERN releases the Web software into the public domain. By March 1994, RFC 1591 already describes .com as a much enlarged category intended for companies. In the same document, .org remains the category for organizations that do not fit elsewhere.

Interpretation. As the Web spreads, an address can become a shop window, a service and a public identity. Reading .com as a symbol of commercial presence belongs to this later history of use, rather than its technical origins. A suffix's original purpose does not exhaust its meaning.

CERN · The birth of the Web ↗IETF · RFC 1591, Domain Name System Structure and Delegation (1994) ↗

2000 and 2004 rounds · later introductions; .mobi revised in 2017

People, communities and ways to connect

Documented fact. In 2000, ICANN selects seven new proposals, including .name and .coop. The 2003–2004 process brings .cat for the Catalan linguistic and cultural community and .mobi for mobile access. In 2017, ICANN approves .mobi's conversion to a standard gTLD without retaining its mobile charter.

Interpretation. Names begin to declare who we are, where we belong and how we connect. .mobi also preserves an expectation later recast in its rules: a documented transformation that does not, by itself, establish commercial failure.

ICANN · New TLDs: FAQs (17 November 2000) ↗IANA · Report on the Delegation of .CAT (2005) ↗ICANN · .MOBI Sponsorship Charter (2005) ↗ICANN · Board minutes, resolution 2017.03.16.04 ↗

May 2010 · first internationalized ccTLD delegations

An address can end in our own script

Documented fact. On 5 May 2010, ICANN announces the first internationalized ccTLDs delegated into the root: Arabic names for Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Requests had opened in November 2009. These are not TLDs from the 2012 round; they follow the dedicated country-code process.

Interpretation. Belonging is expressed through more than territory or activity. It can also appear in the script a person reads and uses to communicate. This is a concrete step toward a more linguistically plural network, although technical availability alone does not measure effective inclusion.

ICANN · First IDN ccTLDs Available (5 May 2010) ↗

2012 round · delegations from 2013; launches and use in different years

Cities and brands enter the same space

Documented fact. The 2012 round receives 1,930 applications, including geographic proposals and names in other scripts. That same round brings .berlin, publicly available in March 2014, and .google, restricted to Google and its affiliates. .google is delegated in September 2014; Google dates its first use to 2016.

Interpretation. The map expands: urban identities and control of a brand coexist within one expansion. These are overlapping projects enabled by the same rules, not eras replacing one another. The gap between application, delegation and use reveals the time needed to turn a name into a presence.

ICANN · New gTLD Reveal Day (13 June 2012) ↗ICANN · Delegated Strings, 2012 round ↗ICANN / dotBERLIN · .BERLIN case study ↗Google Registry · .google Domain Registration Policy ↗Google Registry · 3 lessons learned from launching .google (2025) ↗

2012 round · .bank agreement in 2014; current requirements consulted in 2026

A name can promise verified membership

Documented fact. The .bank agreement sets banking-community rules and eligibility verification. The current registry restricts registration, including regulated banks and certain related organizations.

Interpretation. A suffix can set an access boundary as well as name an activity. Trust is a project supported by rules here: these sources neither measure users’ trust nor establish an absence of abuse.

ICANN · .bank Registry Agreement, Specification 12 (2014) ↗fTLD · .Bank registrant eligibility ↗

2012 round · .blog opens in 2016; WordPress.com subdomains in 2018

Publishing a voice, within a platform

Documented fact. Nominet announces .blog general availability on 21 November 2016. In November 2018, WordPress.com offers free addresses beneath names such as food.blog: subdomains, rather than independent .blog domain registrations.

Interpretation. Web participation gains a recognizable name while access can remain mediated by a platform. A personal address does not imply infrastructure control: editorial openness and technical dependence can coexist.

Nominet · .blog general availability (21 November 2016) ↗WordPress.com · Free .blog subdomains (28 November 2018; updated 2024) ↗

Current reuse of .ai · 2026 applications published on 7 October

Changing times give existing names new meanings

Documented fact. .ai remains Anguilla's country code, while its official registry also promotes it as a sign of innovation and artificial intelligence. On 7 October 2026, ICANN publishes applications for the new round: proposals still under review, rather than newly operational TLDs.

Interpretation. A name can express the present without being newly created. .ai shows a new cultural association attached to existing infrastructure; the 2026 applications reveal what participants would like to name next. Origin, aspiration and use are three traces to read together.

IANA · .ai, country-code TLD for Anguilla ↗.ai · Official Registry Operator Website ↗ICANN · Applications revealed, 2026 round (7 October 2026) ↗

TLDs are not a complete mirror of society. They show who was able to request a name, what space they obtained and how that name was used. The most revealing trajectory emerges where these three histories meet.

How to read this trajectory

Each stage separates documented facts from interpretation; the selected examples are not a census. The reproducible census below includes every string from the sources collected for this project and applies the same present-day classification vocabulary across the different rounds. Semantic assignment is incomplete: names without a category remain in the corpus, and counts depend on rule coverage. This reading does not automatically reconstruct each name's historical meaning or represent the full range of online identities. Application, delegation and public availability are distinct events; the counts do not measure use or adoption.

Method and limits

Counts use distinct strings, not applications: competing applicants do not increase a name’s weight. Categories may overlap. Themes describe the string, not the applicant’s industry or social impact. Official 2026 brand, community and geographic fields are not projected backwards onto previous rounds. Replacement records and variant-only applications are retained in the census but excluded from the main 2026 comparison. Missing classification is not evidence that a phenomenon is absent.

Dated local corpora, not a universal list of every name ever proposed. The 2026 applications express intentions and do not establish future delegation or use.

READING

What is a dot?

A domain is a technical identifier with legal, economic, institutional and cultural dimensions. These eight perspectives explain what can gather around one name.
01

Address

A human-readable identifier that helps users and software find Internet resources.

02

Contract

A registration exists through agreements among registrant, registrar and registry.

03

Market

Names can carry retail prices, premium pricing, renewals and secondary-market value.

04

Jurisdiction

Eligibility, policies and legal duties vary across namespaces and operators.

05

Identity

A domain can accumulate reputation and become a persistent identifier for a person, place or institution.

06

Trust boundary

Verification, DNSSEC and registry rules can add trust signals around a name.

07

Cultural sign

Communities and language can give a TLD meanings that its original designation never anticipated.

08

Political object

Country codes, city names and allocation disputes can reflect institutions, borders and public authority.

The dot is technical. What societies build around it is not.
A useful way to read a TLD is to ask which layer is doing the work: addressing, allocation, governance, trust, market value, identity or cultural meaning.
FACTREADING

One word, two naming systems: .bit

The frozen 2026 secondary index shows 11 ICANN applications for .bit. Namecoin already uses .bit in a separate blockchain-based naming system. It is not a delegated TLD in the ICANN global DNS root and ordinary DNS resolvers do not automatically use Namecoin's records. This is a namespace collision risk to explain, not a claim that Namecoin is one of the 11 applicants.

FACT

How Internet domains actually work

The essential concepts for navigating Internet domains, DNS and Internet governance.
www.example.com

In www.example.com, .com is the top-level domain (TLD). “example” is the second-level label; the name registered under .com is example.com. “www” is an additional label identifying a subdomain.

.
Root

The invisible top of the DNS hierarchy.

.com
Top-level domain

The final part: .ch, .com, .org.

example
Second-level label

Here, “example” is the label immediately to the left of .com. Together they form the domain name example.com.

www
Optional label

An optional label added in front of the registered name. In www.example.com, “www” can identify a specific site or service; it is not part of the TLD.

FACT

Who does what?

The Internet has no single “owner”. It works through distinct roles, contracts and technical coordination.
POLICY

ICANN

Coordinates policies and contracts for generic top-level domains through a global multistakeholder model.

ROOT

IANA / PTI

Acts as Root Zone Manager: PTI receives and validates TLD change requests and manages the authoritative delegation data for the DNS root.

MAINTAIN

Root Zone Maintainer

Verisign implements validated root-zone changes as the operational Root Zone Maintainer under contract with ICANN.

GOVERNANCE

Registry operator

Operates a TLD and its authoritative registry database. gTLD operators work under ICANN registry agreements; ccTLD governance arrangements differ.

TECH

Registry Service Provider

Provides critical technical registry services such as DNS and registration infrastructure for the registry operator.

RETAIL

Registrar

For gTLDs, an ICANN-accredited registrar provides the direct registration channel to registrants. ccTLDs use their own registry and registrar models.

USER

Registrant

The person or organization that registers and uses a domain name under the TLD.

IANA · Root Zone Manager / Maintainer ↗ICANN · accredited registrars ↗
FACT

What do you actually get when you register a domain?

Registration is not the purchase of a piece of the Internet. A registrant enters a contractual relationship, and the name remains subject to renewal, registry policy and the applicable lifecycle.
01Available

The name is not currently registered and may be eligible under the registry policy.

→
02Registered

A registrant enters an agreement through a registrar and the registry records the name.

↺ Renewal loop→
03Expired

If the registration term ends, post-expiration rules apply. Renewal or restoration may still be possible depending on policy and timing.

If the registrar deletes an applicable gTLD registration
04Redemption period

If an applicable gTLD registration is deleted by the registrar, it enters a 30-day redemptionPeriod during which restoration may be possible.

→
05PendingDelete

If it is not restored during redemptionPeriod, the name enters pendingDelete for five days and cannot be restored.

→
06Available again

After purge from the registry database, the name may become available for registration again under the registry policy.

This is a simplified gTLD-oriented map, not one universal lifecycle. Expiration does not automatically equal deletion. Registry, registrar and ccTLD policies can differ.
ICANN · renewal & expiration ↗ICANN · EPP status codes ↗
READING

The economics of the dot

The same domain can sit inside several markets at once: registration, renewal, premium pricing, registry services and secondary-market trading.
RegistrantChooses the name and pays the retail registration or renewal price.
→
RegistrarProvides the retail channel and submits registration transactions to the registry.
→
RegistryOperates the TLD database and sets the registry-side commercial and policy model within its framework.
↗
ICANN layerFor gTLDs, contractual and fee relationships also sit above the registry and registrar ecosystem.
AftermarketExisting registrations can acquire resale value independently of the registry’s wholesale price.
A domain price is not one thing. Wholesale, retail, premium and aftermarket value belong to different layers.
FACT

How a new TLD is born

The 2026 process is not “apply and receive”. It is a staged public process.
01
Application

Applicant files the application and pays the required fee.

02
Reveal

ICANN publishes public application data and identifies identical-string contention.

03
Input & objections

Community input, formal objections and relevant government advice can enter the process.

04
Evaluation

String, applicant, operational, financial and technical components are evaluated.

05
Contention

If multiple applicants seek the same or confusingly similar string, the contention must be resolved.

06
Contract

A successful applicant signs the Base Registry Agreement with ICANN.

07
Delegation

After onboarding and technical checks, IANA/PTI processes the delegation request and the Root Zone Maintainer implements the validated change in the DNS root.

08
Launch

Only then can the registry move toward actually using and allocating names under the TLD.

Official explainer · ICANN Applicant Journey ↗
FACTREADING

Two different questions: what kind of application is it, and who can register?

ICANN application types and day-to-day registration access are different axes. A namespace can be geographic, community or brand-oriented and still impose very different access rules.

2026 application types / designations

General

An application that does not fall into a specialized application type.

Geographic Name

A specialized application for a string meeting the 2026 geographic-name criteria and applicable support or non-objection requirements.

Reserved Name

A specialized application involving a name reserved under the 2026 Applicant Guidebook rules.

Community

A specialized application linked to a clearly delineated community and the additional commitments required for that designation.

.Brand

A specialized application for an eligible string tied to a registered trademark and qualifying brand operator.

IDN

An application for a TLD string represented in a script supported through the Internationalized Domain Name framework.

Variant string

An application involving variant strings evaluated together with the primary applied-for string.

Government / IGO

An application submitted by a government or intergovernmental organization and treated as specialized.

Applicant Support

An application from an applicant qualifying for assistance through the Applicant Support Program is treated as specialized.

Operational access model

.com

Open registration

A namespace broadly open to eligible registrants under standard registry rules.

.bank

Restricted / verified

A namespace where eligibility must be verified; .BANK is an example for regulated banking organizations.

These labels describe ICANN’s 2026 application designations. Historical TLDs are not presented here as if they were 2026 examples. “Open” or “restricted” instead describes practical registration access after delegation.

Precise words, clear concepts

The essential concepts for navigating domains, DNS and Internet governance.
FACT
More precise

A top-level domain is the final part of an Internet address, such as .ch or .com.

Not the same thing

A TLD is simply a new website address.

FACT
More precise

ICANN coordinates the global domain-name system and the new-gTLD process.

Not the same thing

ICANN is the government or owner of the Internet.

FACT

Essential glossary

The terms that make the Explorer easier to read. Official ICANN/IANA vocabulary is kept separate from Connecting the Dots methodology fields.
ICANN / IANA termProject methodology
ICANNICANN / IANA term

Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers. A nonprofit public-benefit organization that coordinates the Internet’s unique identifier systems and supports related policy development, including the DNS.

Source ↗
IANA / Internet Assigned Numbers AuthorityICANN / IANA term

Functions that maintain authoritative registries for the Internet’s globally unique technical identifiers, including domain names, numbers and protocol parameters. The IANA functions are performed by PTI, an ICANN affiliate.

Source ↗
DNS / Domain Name SystemICANN / IANA term

The Internet’s distributed, hierarchical naming system. It lets clients query readable names such as example.com and obtain information needed to reach associated services, such as IP addresses.

Source ↗
TLD / Top-Level DomainICANN / IANA term

A domain immediately below the DNS root, such as .ch or .com. The string .lugano is an application in the 2026 round and is not yet delegated.

Source ↗
DNS root / Root zoneICANN / IANA term

The highest level of the DNS hierarchy. The root zone contains the delegations of TLDs recognized by the global DNS.

Source ↗
gTLD / Generic Top-Level DomainICANN / IANA term

The category of generic top-level domains, such as .com, distinct from ccTLDs and the infrastructure domain .arpa. It includes legacy extensions and new gTLDs introduced through ICANN programs.

Source ↗
ccTLD / Country-Code Top-Level DomainICANN / IANA term

A TLD associated with a country or territory, normally based on a two-letter ISO 3166-1 code or an approved IDN string.

Source ↗
IDN / Internationalized Domain NameICANN / IANA term

A domain name that uses characters beyond the basic ASCII set, for example characters from non-Latin scripts.

Source ↗
A-label / PunycodeICANN / IANA term

A-label: the ASCII representation of an IDNA-valid IDN label, always beginning with xn--. Punycode is the algorithm used to encode the part following that prefix.

Source ↗
Name server / Server DNSICANN / IANA term

A DNS server that answers queries about a domain name. An authoritative name server hosts the official records for the DNS zone for which it is responsible.

Source ↗
RDAP / Registration Data Access ProtocolICANN / IANA term

An HTTP-based protocol for accessing current domain-name registration and IP-address data. It was designed as a replacement for WHOIS, with standardized formats, HTTPS and internationalization support.

Source ↗
WHOISICANN / IANA term

A protocol and set of services historically used to query domain-name registration data. RDAP was designed to replace the protocol with more modern, standardized access.

Source ↗
ApplicantICANN / IANA term

The entity that submits an application to ICANN for a new gTLD.

Source ↗
ApplicationICANN / IANA term

The formal application for a new gTLD. An application is not the same as delegation of the string into the DNS root.

Source ↗
Application roundICANN / IANA term

The complete sequence of stages through which ICANN processes applications received during a specific submission period.

Source ↗
DelegationICANN / IANA term

The technical insertion of a TLD into the DNS root. Only after delegation does the string become active in the global naming system.

Source ↗
Registry operatorICANN / IANA term

The entity that operates the TLD and its authoritative registry database. For gTLDs it operates under a Registry Agreement with ICANN.

Source ↗
Registry Service Provider (RSP)ICANN / IANA term

The provider of critical technical services needed to run the registry, distinct from the entity holding registry-operator responsibility.

Source ↗
RegistrarICANN / IANA term

For gTLDs, an ICANN-accredited intermediary that provides users with the channel for registering domain names. ccTLDs may use different models.

Source ↗
RegistrantICANN / IANA term

The person or organization that registers a domain name.

Source ↗
Registry AgreementICANN / IANA term

The contractual agreement between ICANN and the registry operator of a gTLD.

Source ↗
Contention setICANN / IANA term

A group of applications for identical or sufficiently similar strings that cannot all proceed without first resolving competition among them.

Source ↗
String contentionICANN / IANA term

The situation in which more than one qualified application competes for the same string or for strings considered confusingly similar.

Source ↗
GAC AdviceICANN / IANA term

Advice from the Governmental Advisory Committee to the ICANN Board concerning one or more applications or public-policy matters.

Source ↗
Name collisionICANN / IANA term

A situation in which a name intended to be resolved in one naming system is instead resolved in another, potentially causing unexpected behavior or operational risk.

Source ↗
Application outcomeProject methodology

A Connecting the Dots methodology field describing the documented outcome of an application separately from contention and controversy. A blank field means the outcome is not proven in the local corpus.

Outcome reasonProject methodology

A methodology field recording, only when supported by a source, the reason for an outcome, such as withdrawal, non-selection, public policy or technical risk.

Governance controversyProject methodology

A Connecting the Dots editorial category for substantive conflicts over rights, legitimacy, public interest, control or conditions of use of a string. It is not the same as contention.

FACTREADING

Who can actually pull which lever?

A website, a domain registration, DNS resolution and browser access are different layers. Different actors can intervene at different points; no single organization “controls the Internet”.
01

Hosting provider

Can remove or disable content or infrastructure it hosts.

02

DNS provider

Can stop serving authoritative DNS or alter the zone it operates.

03

Registrar

Maintains the registrant relationship and submits registration changes to the registry.

04

Registry operator

Maintains the TLD registry and processes additions, changes or deletions under applicable rules.

05

Browser / security layer

Can warn, block or distrust a destination without changing the registration itself.

06

ICANN

Coordinates gTLD policy and contracts, but is not a general-purpose content regulator or Internet police force.

Same website, different levers.
Taking content offline, suspending a registration, changing DNS and blocking access are not the same action. Governance starts by identifying the layer.
ICANN states that it does not control Internet content and is not a general-purpose website takedown authority.
ICANN · registry operator ↗ICANN · accredited registrars ↗ICANN · website content ↗
.lugano · applied caseWhat those general rules mean for Lugano’s 2026 application.
FACT

From the general rule to .lugano

The .lugano application follows the same process described above. Until evaluation, contracting and delegation are completed, .lugano remains an application and is not an active TLD.
VISION
Hypothetical example
www.servizi.lugano
If .lugano is delegated, the same DNS structure could produce addresses such as servizi.lugano or www.servizi.lugano. This illustrates the hierarchy; it is not a live service.

For .lugano: what the registry could govern, and what it would not mean

VISION

What the registry could govern

  • Eligibility and allocation policies for names under .lugano, within ICANN rules and applicable law.
  • Reserved names, launch phases and local governance choices.
  • Registration-policy and security requirements for names operating under .lugano.
FACT

What it would not mean

  • Lugano does not “own the Internet” or control .ch, .com or other TLDs.
  • An application is not an assignment: .lugano is not active until the process, contract and delegation are complete.
  • ICANN does not operate the City’s websites; it coordinates the global naming system and the gTLD contractual framework.

Speaking precisely about .lugano

Two distinctions that matter while the application is still in process.
FACT
More precise

The City of Lugano has applied for the new top-level domain .lugano.

Not the same thing

Lugano has obtained / owns the .lugano domain.

VISION
More precise

If successful, .lugano could become a governed namespace under rules defined by its registry operator within the ICANN framework.

Not the same thing

Anyone will automatically be able to register any .lugano name.

When a TLD becomes infrastructureInvisible DNSScripts & UADifferent roots
READING

When a TLD becomes infrastructure

Some namespaces went far beyond naming. They added eligibility, verification, security rules, public-interest governance or shared digital services.
01
Name

A memorable address.

02
Qualified community

Rules define who belongs.

03
Verified identity

Eligibility is checked.

04
Security baseline

Technical requirements become part of the namespace.

05
Shared services

The TLD becomes a platform for common services.

READING
Some of the clearest examples show that a TLD can encode more than a name: eligibility, identity, security, community rules and shared services.
FACT
.post
Shared services

A TLD with a service layer

The UPU vets registrants, mandates a cybersecurity framework and operates trust.post, a Shared Services Platform for the postal and logistics sector.

Primary source ↗
FACT
.cat
Civic infrastructure

A domain that funds a digital commons

The .cat registry reinvests its revenues in digital rights, tools and projects for the Catalan-speaking community, describing the wider mission as civic infrastructure.

Primary source ↗
FACT
.bank / .insurance
Verified trust

Security rules encoded into membership

Resolving .bank and .insurance domains must implement requirements such as DNSSEC, TLS and email authentication. The suffix is designed to signal a higher-trust environment.

Primary source ↗
FACT
.gov
Verified public identity

The suffix itself is an institutional credential

Only verified U.S. government organizations can register .gov. CISA verifies eligibility and the identity of requesters before approval.

Primary source ↗
FACT
.pharmacy
External qualification

A domain tied to accreditation

A registrant must first demonstrate compliance with NABP standards and receive accreditation. The domain is connected to an external qualification process.

Primary source ↗
FACT
.eco
Profile + commitment

Activation requires a profile and a pledge

A .eco registration remains on hold until the registrant affirms eligibility, completes an Eco Profile and makes a public environmental commitment.

Primary source ↗
FACT
.swiss
Qualified namespace

A namespace reserved for a defined community

.swiss is restricted to the Swiss community and applies eligibility rules linking the registrant and the requested name to Switzerland.

Primary source ↗
FACTREADING

The invisible DNS

The DNS already does much more than turn names into IP addresses. It routes mail, publishes authentication data and certificate-authorization policy, advertises services and can carry cryptographic trust.
MX

Mail routing

MX records tell sending systems which mail servers handle email for a domain.

Source ↗
SPF · DKIM · DMARC

Email authentication

SPF, DKIM and DMARC use DNS-published data to help receivers evaluate authorized and authenticated mail.

Source 1 ↗Source 2 ↗Source 3 ↗
CAA

Certificate authorization

CAA records publish which certificate authorities are authorized to issue certificates for a domain.

Source ↗
DNSSEC

Integrity and origin authentication

DNSSEC signs DNS data so resolvers can validate its origin and integrity through a chain of trust.

Source ↗
SRV

Service discovery

SRV records can advertise the hostname and port of services associated with a domain.

Source ↗
SVCB · HTTPS

Connection hints

SVCB and HTTPS records can publish service endpoints and connection parameters before a client connects.

Source ↗
The DNS is already an infrastructure layer for routing, discovery and trust. “Beyond the domain” is therefore an extension of existing capabilities, not a departure from what DNS already does.
FACT

The Internet is not written only in Latin characters

Internationalized Domain Names allow top-level domains in non-ASCII scripts. Universal Acceptance is the practical requirement that browsers, email systems and applications actually accept them.
.中国.السعودية.ไทย.рф.ευ
Universal Acceptance

A name can be valid in the global DNS and still fail in an application that assumes old ASCII-only or short-TLD rules. Universal Acceptance is about removing those technical barriers.

Global naming requires more than delegation. Software has to recognize the names people are actually allowed to use.
IANA · root database ↗ICANN · Universal Acceptance ↗
FACTREADING

One dot, different universes

A dot-separated string can look like a domain while belonging to a different naming regime. Visual similarity does not mean the same root, resolver or governance system.
DNS
Public DNS root

.com, .ch, .中国 and other delegated TLDs live in the globally coordinated DNS root.

RFC
Special-use DNS names

.test, .localhost, .invalid, .onion and home.arpa have standards-defined special behavior; they are not ordinary public-root TLD registrations.

.test · .localhost · .onion · home.arpa
ALT
Alternative naming systems

.eth is part of Ethereum Name Service; Handshake describes itself as an experimental peer-to-peer root naming system. These are different naming systems, not ICANN-root TLDs.

.eth · Handshake
Looks like a domain ≠ is a public DNS TLD.
The important question is not only what comes after the dot, but which root and resolution system gives that label meaning.
IANA · special-use names ↗ENS · protocol ↗Handshake ↗

READING

A second generation of city TLDs?

The first wave was largely about identity, locality and registration. A 2026 city namespace could also be designed around trusted public services, verifiable identity, machine-readable governance and interaction with AI agents. That is an editorial hypothesis, not an ICANN classification.

FACTREADING

.helsinki: a city can also give up its TLD

In 2026 Helsinki initiated the voluntary termination of its registry agreement. This is a concrete counterpoint for anyone considering a city TLD: securing a delegation and sustaining it over time are different decisions.

Read the documented timeline and status →

CITIES, RULES AND OUTCOMES

Who governs a city's domain?

Comparative analysis, not a ranking

A territorial extension can be governed in different ways. What matters is who sets the rules, answers for outcomes, pays and provides continuity if the project struggles. Registry responsibility and technical operations need not sit with the same organisation.

Public authority responsible

The authority remains responsible while specialist providers may run the technology.

Policy autonomy still requires expertise, resources and continuity.

Publicly owned company

The city steers and oversees a corporate operator.

Its mandate, corporate governance, costs and accountability need to be explicit.

Community organisation

An organisation represents cultural, territorial or community interests.

Representation, access and long-term financial capacity must be tested.

Contracted private operator

A business operates the registry under arrangements with the territorial authority.

Public control depends on enforceable commitments, scrutiny and exit provisions.

Four cases, not four comparable operating results

.lugano · 2026 application

The City of Lugano is the applicant. A staged opening and a territorial connection are declared; ICANN approval and final registration criteria remain outstanding.

Città di Lugano · progetto e FAQ (08.10.2026) ↗ICANN APS · CDL2651T-T31516 ↗

.bremen · policy adopted in 2026

The Senate supports external applicants through agreements: up to 300 protected names reserved without charge, up to 300 further names in a paid priority phase, an exclusion list and conflict mediation. These are intended contractual conditions, not measured operating outcomes.

Senat Bremen · 14.07.2026, pp. 2–4 ↗

.paris · delegated TLD

IANA identifies the City of Paris as sponsoring organisation and AFNIC as technical contact. Public responsibility can coexist with specialist technical delivery.

IANA · .paris ↗

.nyc · delegated TLD

IANA identifies the City of New York as sponsoring organisation and GoDaddy Registry as administrative and technical contact. The technical provider alone does not identify who bears registry responsibility.

IANA · .nyc ↗

Ask who sets prices and eligibility, reserves names, handles abuse and appeals, funds security and continuity, and retains public powers when an operator changes. No legal form answers all those questions by itself.

Editorial review: 17 October 2026

CITIES, RULES AND OUTCOMES

Success is more than names sold

Analytical proposal, not adopted policy

A proposed evaluation framework to define before launch, with explicit denominators, periods and sources. No performance values are assigned to .lugano here.

Actual use

The share used for websites, mail or services, distinguishing parking, redirects and defensive holdings. No website does not necessarily mean no use.

Persistence

Renewals by cohort and term, departures and continued use. Defensive renewal alone does not demonstrate public value.

Public value

Recognisable services, accessibility, participation and documented benefits for users and the territory. These require evaluation, not just address counts.

Sustainability

Recurring costs, income, subsidy dependence, security and continuity. The application fee is not the whole cost of the project.

READING

The geography of power in the DNS

Rules, registry contracts, technical infrastructure and applicant demand have different geographies. Explore each layer separately to understand where decisions and capabilities concentrate.

Power is a stack, not a dot on a map

Five layers matter, and they describe different things. Collapsing them into one “center of the Internet” would be neat, dramatic and wrong.

01

Rules

ICANN’s global multistakeholder process develops policy; ICANN org implements the contractual and program framework for gTLDs.

02

Root coordination

PTI validates root-zone change requests; Verisign implements validated changes as Root Zone Maintainer. Root serving itself is distributed among independent operators worldwide.

03

Registry contracts

Each gTLD registry operator holds contractual responsibility for its namespace. Some operators hold large portfolios of registry agreements.

04

Technical backend

Registry Service Providers supply registry, DNS and DNSSEC infrastructure across many TLDs. Technical concentration can differ sharply from ownership.

05

Demand

Applicants decide which strings are worth pursuing. Their public business locations reveal where commercial, civic and institutional demand originates.

FACT

Mapping and measuring power

Switch layers to see institutional coordination, evaluated technical supply and applicant demand. They overlap, but they are not the same kind of power.

READING

Why does concentration emerge?

Registry operations carry substantial fixed costs in infrastructure, security, compliance and registrar distribution. A broad portfolio lets an operator reuse the same backend and sales channels, spread risk across niche strings and grow further through acquisitions. Donuts explicitly cited economies of scale as a core reason for applying for hundreds of strings in 2012.

Applications ≠ awarded TLDs ≠ registry agreements ≠ TLD portfolio ≠ RSP-managed TLDs ≠ Internet governance. The numbers belong to different layers and must not be added together.
FACT

Two different forms of concentration

Counting TLD strings and counting domains registered underneath them produces two very different pictures of scale.

Identity Digital
~300TLDs in Identity Digital’s portfolio · breadth across namespacesICANN ↗
Verisign
179.1M.com + .net registrations · Q2 2026
Root Zone Maintainer · operator of A-root and J-root
Verisign · Q2 2026 ↗IANA · root servers ↗
READING

There is no single league table of “Internet power”. Identity Digital concentrates portfolio breadth across many TLDs; Verisign combines exceptional registration depth under .com/.net with important root operational roles. Neither measure is equivalent to control over ICANN policy.

FACT

The root is coordinated through a small number of institutions, but served globally

PTI manages root-zone changes and Verisign maintains the root-zone file, while 12 independent root-server operators serve 13 logical root identities through thousands of physical instances worldwide. Institutional coordination and physical delivery therefore have very different geographies.

1212 independent root-server operators
1313 logical root-server identities (A–M)
2,0452,045 operational root-server instances as of 12 Sep 2026

READING

What “Internet power” means here

The dashboard can show where policy institutions, root functions, registry contracts, applicant headquarters and technical providers cluster. It cannot reduce Internet governance to headquarters, or equate a large TLD portfolio with control over ICANN policy or the DNS root.

FACTREADING

A country code can become a digital natural resource

Semantic accidents can create real economic value. Anguilla’s .AI is the clearest current example: a two-letter country code became globally aligned with artificial intelligence.
.ai
EC$253.6M2026 Anguilla budget estimate · Domain Name RegistrationEC$253.6 million · budget estimate, not realized revenue
Tiny geography, global namespace.
The economic value comes from a global meaning that the country did not invent but can govern and monetize. A ccTLD can therefore behave like a scarce national digital asset.

The economics of the dot

What is a dot worth?

TLDs are naming infrastructure, but they can also create public revenue, recurring registry income, scarcity rents, acquisition value and financial barriers to entry. These cases keep unlike metrics separate rather than forcing them into one league table.

Selection rule: each case illustrates a distinct economic mechanism and is supported by attributable financial or institutional evidence. Revenue, valuation, auction price and public receipts are not interchangeable measures.

Scope and sources for each round

2000

47 applications received, 44 evaluated: US$2.2 million is reconstructed as 44 × US$50,000. Two applications had not paid and one was withdrawn over confidentiality. ICANN's February 2001 budget lists the same total as projected actual revenue; a separately verified final collection figure for the round is not established here.

ICANN — New TLD Application Instructions, 15 August 2000, §§ I28–I29 ↗ICANN — TLD Application Review Update, 23 October 2000 ↗ICANN — FY2001–2002 Preliminary Budget, 19 February 2001, Schedule A ↗

2004

Ten applications at US$45,000 each. ICANN explicitly reports US$450,000 collected in its 7 October 2004 report to the U.S. Department of Commerce.

ICANN — Tenth Status Report to the U.S. Department of Commerce, 7 October 2004, p. 10 ↗

2012

About US$357 million collected at launch, according to ICANN's program review. Its later FY12–FY23 statement reports about US$360 million in fees, US$52 million in refunds and US$308 million net: this covers a different period and is not the net of the initial US$357 million alone.

ICANN — New gTLD Program Implementation Review, 29 January 2016, § 8.3.1; p. 183 ↗ICANN — FY26 Budget, May 2025, p. 29, § 5.1.1 ↗

2026

1,615 is the official total published on 7 October; the public export analysed contains 1,614 applications plus replacement records. There are 51 ASP applications, with planned discounts of 75–85%, and waivers for some variants. Actual collections were not found in the sources reviewed: multiplying 1,615 × US$227,000 does not establish them.

How to read the figures

Nominal amounts in U.S. dollars. The fee pays for application evaluation and does not guarantee a TLD. Documented totals and reconstructed figures are identified separately. Initial collections, refunds and multiyear statements cover different scopes; they are not profit. Conditional evaluation fees and annual registry fees are outside this comparison.

Auction proceeds are a separate category and are not included in application fees.

Editorial review · 19 October 2026

FACTREADING

The competition hidden inside 980 strings

The 263 preliminary identical-string contention sets contain 891 applications. That is 55.2% of the secondary index's 1,614 applications, although the 263 contested strings are only 26.8% of the 980 primary strings in the frozen nTLDData inventory. In internet.Best's applicant ranking, the five largest portfolios account for 491 applications, 30.4% of its 1,614-record base. Contention is not an awarded TLD, and a filed application is not a revenue forecast.

ICANN · preliminary contention CSV ↗ internet.Best · applicant portfolios ↗ nTLDData · primary strings ↗
DERIVEDREADING

Words are a market. Not yet an outcome.

In the 2026 round, competition for identical strings reveals applicants' economic expectations. Filing does not mean winning a TLD, and contention is not a direct measure of future demand.

Scarcity forms around a word

Our analysis of the 7 October APS snapshot finds 263 exact-primary-string groups comprising 891 applications. These are analytical groups, not ICANN's definitive contention sets. Replacements and subsequent evaluations can change the picture.

Intercap: applying as a portfolio strategy

Domain Name Wire (7 October) attributes 71 applications to Intercap Registry: 58 for strings with identical-string rivals and 13 without such rivals in its analysis. These press figures require reconciliation with APS application IDs before being treated as official totals. This illustrates a portfolio strategy, not completed acquisitions.

Brands, products and AI agent identities: different logics

ICANN reports 333 brand applications on Reveal Day. A corporate brand, a product name and a possible digital-agent identity are different strategies. Using TLDs as trust infrastructure for AI agents remains a hypothesis, not an established result.

AI and crypto appear in the 2026 subset

The 2026 subset contains records classified under AI and crypto; the equivalent editorial categories have no records in 2012. This describes the vocabulary and classification of these subsets. It does not mean those technologies did not exist in 2012, or establish future adoption.

Finance: institutions and generic terms

The finance category combines identified organisations with generic financial terms. Corporate or brand names and references to a financial market express different naming strategies; their combined share does not count the financial institutions participating in the round.

Media and communications: a smaller share of the subset

In the historical classification, media and communications account for 13.7% of the 2012 subset and 8.0% of the 2026 subset. The category has a smaller relative share; this does not establish a decline in those industries or in their economic value.

Identity and digital trust: a larger share of the subset

The cybersecurity, identity and trust category accounts for 0.9% of the 2012 classified subset and 5.4% of the 2026 subset. That is a larger share in this map, not a measure of growth in the industry. Any future practical value of the names would depend on governance, services and actual use.

Financial names: brands and shared terms

A bank's own TLD and a term such as .bank describe very different allocation models. A string's sector does not establish who may register, who governs it, or whether it will be delegated.

Method

Aruba: why 39 and 20 can both be correct

Aruba announced 39 applied-for strings including replacements; the frozen secondary index lists 20 live primary applications for Aruba PEC S.p.A. These are different units and scopes. Adding or comparing them as equivalent counts would be misleading.

Who controls a name: the applicant, the corporate group or the eventual registry operator?
What the ranking really reveals
Large application portfolios reveal a strategy, not a guaranteed market position. Applications can fail, enter contention, be withdrawn or remain undelegated. Concentration at application stage is not identical to concentration of functioning TLD registries.

The 2012 and 2026 figures are not a directly comparable corporate-group ranking. The 2026 counts use 1,614 published applications, including six existing-TLD variant applications; the official reported total is 1,615. They describe the captured applications and their original primary labels, not final confirmed strings or awarded TLDs.

Eight ways money enters the namespace

The same DNS root can generate very different economic relationships.

01

Sovereign digital rent

A country-code namespace becomes a material source of government revenue because global demand attaches value to its two-letter code.

02

National contract revenue

A state monetizes its ccTLD through a commercial registry or marketing agreement rather than operating a mass-market registrar business itself.

03

Operator acquisition

The company operating one or more namespaces is bought, turning expected registry cash flows into a transaction value.

04

Recurring registry economics

Large installed bases and annual renewals can create highly recurring infrastructure revenue, but company-level results must not be mislabeled as revenue from one TLD.

05

Valuation & regulation

A registry contract can underpin billion-dollar valuation while price controls, public-interest duties and change-of-control review shape the asset.

06

Scarcity & auction

When multiple applicants want the same string, scarcity can be converted into an auction price before the registry has sold a single domain.

072012 ROUND · HISTORICAL · PROHIBITED IN 2026

Private contention settlement (2012 · historical)

Historical 2012-round mechanism: applicants could receive consideration for withdrawing from contention, so abandoning a string could generate accounting gains. Private contention resolution, including settlement agreements and compensation for withdrawal, is prohibited in the 2026 round.

08

Cost of entry

Application fees and additional evaluation costs determine who can afford to compete for a place in the root.

Economic cases

Read each number in its own accounting context. The purpose is comparison of mechanisms, not a ranking of “most valuable TLDs”.

How expensive is the right to compete for the root?

FACT

The base evaluation fee was US$185,000 in the 2012 round and is US$227,000 per application in the 2026 round, before certain additional fees or support discounts.

US$185,000Base application evaluation fee2012 · USD
US$227,000Base application evaluation fee2026 · USD

The application fee is not a purchase price for a TLD. It is an entry cost into an uncertain evaluation process, and therefore part of the economic barrier to participation.

ICANN — 2012 New gTLD evaluation fee ↗ICANN — 2026 gTLD evaluation fee ↗ICANN — 2026 financial projection templates ↗
FACTREADING

Economic cycles: what applied-for strings reveal (and what they do not)

The dot-com bubble, platform expansion, crypto boom-and-bust cycles and current AI investment frenzy frame successive moments of demand for names. They are different waves, not one inevitable path from a popular term to a profitable registry.

The dot-com bubble: the web before the new rounds

The speculative surge and crash around 2000 occurred before the 2012 mass gTLD application round. Its legacy is a useful warning: a boom in companies, websites or domain prices does not prove that a new top-level registry will succeed.

Crypto: more than one market winter

Between the 2012 and 2026 rounds, crypto experienced repeated booms and contractions. A 2026 string application may signal renewed interest, but does not measure blockchain adoption, registry demand or an applicant's financial resilience.

AI: a different point in the cycle

Generative AI is still undergoing rapid commercialization. The editorial 2026 inventory includes AI-labelled applications, while the 2012 editorial comparison shows none in that category. Different taxonomies and the long gap require caution: names are not economic forecasts.

E-commerce, social networks and the physical economy

Platforms can create demand for recognisable identities without needing a TLD of their own. Conversely, banking, manufacturing, logistics, retail and public institutions may seek branded or sector-restricted namespaces as infrastructure rather than as speculative real estate.

Method: this is a historical interpretation of sectors and digital-market cycles, not proof of causation. Do not equate an application with delegation, actual registry operation, second-level registrations or financial success.
READING

The gTLD cemetery

The economic costs of running a registry also illuminate exits and failed projects. For evidence, chronology and distinct outcomes, continue to the dedicated chapter.

Withdrawn or rejected application; signed contract without delegation; delegated TLD later revoked; registry operator replaced while the TLD persists. These categories must not be merged into a single mortality count.

The social life of the dot

Who belongs after the dot?

TLDs can mark language, territory, identity, professions, rights or community norms. These cases examine what a namespace asks of the people who use it and the community it claims to represent.

This is a curated social reading, not a ranking of “social success”. Registration volume, community value and cultural significance are different things.
Explore who controls Internet access ↗

Names, society and access

Belonging changes over time

Languages, communities, cities and brands coexist in the DNS. Understanding their social meaning requires separating who proposes a name, who may use it and who actually does. The historical comparison connects these levels without treating them as equivalent.

Read the trajectory →

Editorial review · 19 October 2026

FACTREADING

.meow: crowdfunding the infrastructure

The nonprofit dotMeow Foundation raised €121,896 in Kickstarter pledges from 1,838 backers for its proposed .meow registry, against a €80,000 goal. The sum is a crowdfunding campaign result, not an established operating budget, a delegated TLD or proof of ICANN approval. The project illustrates community financing of the naming layer without being automatically equivalent to ICANN's formal Community application category.

ICANN reports 16 Community-based applications. Other applicants can still pursue an explicit social mission without using that formal designation. .meow is a useful example: its nonprofit applicant says it intends to channel surplus registry revenue into queer community projects. That mission should not be confused with ICANN’s application-type label.

Six ways a namespace becomes social

These categories describe different social functions and can overlap within the same TLD.

01

Language & cultural identity

A namespace can give a language or cultural community a visible place in global naming.

02

Civic & territorial belonging

A local nexus can turn a place name into a membership signal rather than generic branding.

03

Identity & representation

A string can become a flag for shared identity, values or representation.

04

Community institutions

Eligibility, verification and governance can bind a namespace to a defined community or institutional movement.

05

Safety, norms & protection

Registry policies can try to create norms, protections or boundaries for vulnerable or sensitive communities.

06

Script & digital inclusion

Internationalized domain names remove the assumption that global naming must be written in Latin characters.

Nine social cases

From linguistic communities to local nexus rules, safety policies and non-Latin scripts.

Same scarcity, different vocabulary

In 2012, .app led with 13 applications and .home and .inc followed with 11. In the current 2026 public data, .agent leads with 13, followed by .bit with 11 and .api, .brand and .hub with 10. Contention still measures scarcity, but the words reveal what each era thought the next Internet would need.

FACT

A major rule changed in 2026

The 2012 round allowed private settlements and private auctions. The 2026 round does not: once contention sets are finalized, the permitted paths are Community Priority Evaluation for eligible Community Applications and ICANN’s New gTLD Auction. Private auctions, joint ventures and other private contention-resolution arrangements are prohibited.

ICANN · Private resolution prohibition ↗
FACTREADING

Who gets to control a word?

Contention is only one version of scarcity. A second question is whether a generic word should ever become an exclusive namespace for one operator.
WORD

Closed generics

ICANN defines a closed generic as a generic term proposed to be operated exclusively for the applicant’s own benefit. For the 2026 round, closed generic applications are not permitted unless and until an approved public-interest methodology exists.

The issue is not “who won the auction?” but whether a generic word should be closed at all.
Some strings are not merely brands. They are pieces of language.
When a namespace corresponds to a generic word, allocation can raise questions about competition, access and public interest that raw contention counts do not capture.
ICANN · Closed Generics ↗
FACTREADING

Applications that didn't make it

Why some applied-for strings never entered the DNS root

This is not a catalogue of 'rejections'. It traces source-backed reasons why selected applications did not reach the DNS root: administrative returns, eligibility failures, non-selection, public-policy decisions, technical-safety blocks and voluntary withdrawals.

One story, one primary home

Contention is competition for the same string. Controversies are conflicts over rights, legitimacy, public interest or control. Application outcomes explain why an application did not reach the root. A case can have more than one dimension, but the editorial story appears once, where its main causal mechanism belongs; the other dimensions remain structured data and cross-links.

2026 status: too early for outcomes

Reveal Day opened the pre-evaluation phase. The Replacement Period runs through 21 October, String Confirmation Day is 17 November, and the Community Input and Objections Period begins only then. The cases below are historical outcomes from earlier rounds, not 2026 results.

ICANN · 2026 milestones ↗

Six different ways an application can stop

'Rejected' is too crude. The process contains different gates, and withdrawal is not a rejection.

01

Administrative gate

The application can fail before substantive evaluation: missing fee, incomplete submission or another formal defect.

02

Support eligibility

An applicant seeking financial assistance can be excluded if it does not meet the support-program criteria.

03

Evaluation failure

Financial, operational, geographic or other criteria can prevent an application from advancing, sometimes after Extended Evaluation.

04

Public-policy stop

Consensus GAC advice can create a strong presumption that an application should not be approved, subject to Board consideration.

05

Technical-safety stop

A string can be stopped because delegation itself is considered unsafe, regardless of who applied for it.

06

Withdrawal

The applicant can leave voluntarily. That is an outcome, but it must not be mislabeled as an ICANN rejection.

FACT

A snapshot at the end of Initial Evaluation. These categories were not all final outcomes, but they show why “not delegated” is not a useful synonym for “rejected”.

Six outcomes worth understanding

Selected examples, not a complete catalogue of every non-delegation. Each isolates a different causal mechanism.

.number · .tel · .phone · .wap
2000
Administrative return
What actually stopped it?

Can a TLD application die before anyone evaluates the idea?

FACT

Yes. In the 2000 round, two of the 47 submitted applications were returned because the USD 50,000 application fee had not been paid. One covered .number / .tel / .phone; the other covered .wap.

READING

Why it belongs here: This is not a dispute and not a judgment on the string. It is the cleanest example of an administrative gate: no valid fee, no substantive review. The later delegation of .tel and .phone also shows that one failed application does not permanently condemn a label.

Outcome

The two 2000 applications were returned. .tel later entered the root through the 2004 sponsored round and .phone through the 2012 round; the original applications did not survive.

ICANN · TLD Application Review Update · 13 Oct 2000 ↗ICANN archive · 2000 application process background ↗IANA · .TEL ↗IANA · .PHONE ↗
.nyc
2000 → 2014
Withdrawal
What actually stopped it?

Is a withdrawal the same thing as being rejected?

FACT

No. ICANN recorded that the 2000 .nyc application was withdrawn because the applicant and ICANN could not agree on the treatment of confidentiality claims.

READING

Why it belongs here: The stop came from the applicant-process relationship, not from a finding that .nyc was an unacceptable TLD. The same label later returned in the 2012 round.

Outcome

The 2000 application disappeared from that round; .nyc was later delegated to the City of New York in 2014.

ICANN · TLD Application Review Update · 13 Oct 2000 ↗IANA · .NYC ↗
.geo
2000
Proof-of-concept selection
What actually stopped it?

Can a proposal be positively evaluated and still not be selected?

FACT

In the 2000 proof-of-concept round, ICANN leadership later described .geo as having received a very positive staff evaluation, while the Board still declined to select it because potential DNS operational risks could not be fully assessed at that experimental stage.

READING

Why it belongs here: The 2000 round was a deliberately small proof of concept, not the later pass/fail pipeline. Non-selection could reflect portfolio design and caution rather than a defective application.

Outcome

.geo was not among the seven proof-of-concept TLDs selected in 2000. It remains outside the root.

ICANN · Roberts testimony · 14 Feb 2001 ↗ICANN archive · 2000 evaluation report ↗
.idn · .ummah
2013
Support eligibility
What actually stopped it?

What happens when financial assistance is itself a gate to the application?

FACT

Only three 2012 applicants requested financial assistance. .kids met the support criteria; .idn and .ummah did not. Under the support rules then in force, the latter two became ineligible for further review and their USD 47,000 fees were to be refunded.

READING

Why it belongs here: The striking point is that the stop did not arise from the semantic validity of .idn or .ummah. It arose from eligibility for a support mechanism that was coupled to continued participation in the round.

Outcome

.idn and .ummah did not continue. Ummah sought reconsideration; the request was denied, while ICANN directed that the concerns raised inform review of the support program.

ICANN · Applicant Support Program update · 12 Mar 2013 ↗ICANN Board · Ummah reconsideration · 18 May 2013 ↗
.gcc
2013–2014
Public-policy stop
What actually stopped it?

Can public-policy advice stop an application before an objection case decides it?

FACT

The GAC issued consensus advice that the .gcc application should not proceed. The New gTLD Program Committee accepted that advice and directed that the application would not be approved.

READING

Why it belongs here: The decisive event was the institutional public-policy gate. A separate legal-rights objection was terminated once the application could no longer proceed; later accountability challenges are secondary to the reason for the stop.

Outcome

.gcc did not proceed in the 2012 round. The applicant’s reconsideration effort was unsuccessful.

ICANN · GAC Beijing advice and responses ↗ICANN NGPC · GCC reconsideration · 30 Jan 2014 ↗
.corp · .home · .mail
2012–2024
Technical-safety stop
What actually stopped it?

What if the problem is the string itself rather than the applicant?

FACT

ICANN identified .corp, .home and .mail as exceptionally high-risk for name collisions with private naming systems. Delegation was deferred, and in 2018 the Board directed that the 2012 applications should not proceed, with full fee refunds available upon withdrawal.

READING

Why it belongs here: This is the clearest technical refusal in the round: the applicant could change, but the collision risk attached to the label. It is therefore fundamentally different from a fight over who deserves the string.

Outcome

None of the three strings was delegated from the 2012 round. ICANN later reaffirmed that prior applicants would receive no preferential right in a future round.

ICANN Board · .CORP / .HOME / .MAIL · 4 Feb 2018 ↗ICANN Board · NCAP decision · 7 Sep 2024 ↗

Disputed Dots

When a string becomes politics.

A contention set means several applicants want the same or a confusingly similar string. A governance dispute is broader: governments, communities, rights holders or applicants can challenge who should operate a name, under what conditions, or whether it should exist at all.

These cases are selected because each exposes a different governance problem. They are not a league table and not a complete catalogue of every dispute in ICANN history.

A failed, returned or withdrawn application is not automatically a governance dispute. Its application outcome is modeled separately from controversy and contention.See application outcomes →

Three 2026 examples: .anime, .agent and .official

The preliminary identical-string sets include .agent (13 applications), .official (8) and .anime (2). The two .anime applicants are Toei Animation, which filed as Community, and Oinkadot. That contrast raises questions about cultural representation and business operation, but neither an objection outcome nor a winner has been determined. A name such as .official also raises trust questions; the string itself grants no public authority and is not evidence of deceptive intent.

FACT

2026 status: applications are public, formal objections are not open yet

The Community Input and Objections Period begins on 17 November 2026 and is scheduled to run through 16 March 2027. The disputes below are therefore precedents that explain the mechanisms, not disputes already decided in the 2026 round.

ICANN · Community input & objections ↗

How a TLD dispute can enter the system

Not every fight is a lawsuit. The new-gTLD process has several formal routes for public-policy concerns, rights claims, community claims, competition and accountability review.

01

GAC advice

Governments can raise public-policy concerns through the Governmental Advisory Committee. Board treatment depends on the form of the advice and the applicable rules.

02

Formal objection

Applications can face String Confusion, Legal Rights, Community or Limited Public Interest objections before independent dispute-resolution providers.

03

Community Priority Evaluation

A qualifying community application in a contention set can seek priority by meeting the Applicant Guidebook criteria.

04

Contention resolution / auction

When identical-string contention remains unresolved, an ICANN auction of last resort can determine which eligible applicant proceeds.

05

Accountability review

Reconsideration and the Independent Review Process test whether ICANN followed its Bylaws, Articles and established procedures.

06

ICANN Board decision

Some disputes ultimately require the Board to weigh application rules, GAC advice, accountability findings and the public interest.

Nine disputes that changed what the dot means

Each case separates the documented record from the question it raises about power, legitimacy and naming.
