.XXX moved from an unsuccessful 2000 proposal to the 2004 sponsored-TLD process. The Board later denied the application; ICM initiated the first IRP request heard by a panel, prevailed in 2010, and .XXX was delegated in 2011.

READING

The case made ICANN accountability tangible: a politically sensitive string became a test of how far Board discretion can go and how that discretion can be reviewed.

Outcome

.XXX was delegated in 2011 to ICM Registry LLC.

.amazon · .亚马逊 · .アマゾン
2012–2020
Geographic identityGovernment adviceAccountabilityGAC adviceAccountability reviewICANN Board decision
The question

Who should be able to operate a TLD string that is also the name of a transnational region?

FACT

Amazon applied for .AMAZON and two IDN equivalents in 2012. Brazil and Peru raised public-policy concerns, GAC consensus advice said the applications should not proceed, and the Board initially accepted that advice. Amazon later prevailed in an IRP; after further Board and government engagement, processing resumed and .AMAZON was delegated in 2020.

READING

The dispute exposed a fundamental collision between trademark-based corporate identity and geographic, cultural and governmental claims over the same word.

Outcome

.AMAZON was delegated in 2020 to Amazon Registry Services, Inc.

Source ↗

Source ↗
2019

After further negotiations and Board consideration, ICANN directed the applications to continue processing.

.AMAZON entered the DNS root.

.africa
2012–2017
Geographic identityGovernment adviceAccountabilityGAC adviceAccountability reviewICANN Board decision
The question

How should a continent-name TLD be awarded when applicants disagree over legitimacy and government support?

FACT

Two applicants sought .AFRICA. GAC consensus advice said DotConnectAfrica’s application should not proceed. DotConnectAfrica later prevailed on important process claims in an IRP, forcing ICANN to resume evaluation. The competing Registry.Africa application ultimately proceeded to delegation.

READING

The dispute became a landmark test of government advice, transparency and ICANN accountability in a geographically symbolic namespace.

Outcome

.AFRICA was delegated in 2017 to ZA Central Registry NPC trading as Registry.Africa.

.web
2012–2026
CompetitionEconomic controlAccountabilityContention resolution / auctionAccountability reviewICANN Board decision
The question

Can funding and future-control arrangements behind an applicant change who is entitled to win a contention auction?

FACT

Seven applicants sought .WEB. Nu Dot Co won the 2016 ICANN auction with a US$135 million bid. Verisign then disclosed that it had funded the bid under an arrangement contemplating future assignment of the registry agreement. Afilias challenged ICANN through a lengthy IRP. .WEB was finally delegated to Verisign in 2026.

READING

A simple contention set turned into a long argument about applicant identity, control, auction integrity and the boundary between financing and substitution.

Outcome

.WEB was delegated in July 2026 to VeriSign, Inc.

.wine · .vin
2012–2015
Geographic identityLegal rightsGovernment adviceGAC adviceICANN Board decision
The question

How far should geographic-indication protections reach inside a global domain namespace?

FACT

.WINE and .VIN triggered sustained government and producer concerns about names such as protected wine regions and appellations. The GAC had no consensus on additional safeguards. ICANN commissioned independent legal analysis and allowed the applications to proceed; both TLDs were delegated in 2015.

READING

The dispute showed that the DNS can become a venue for unresolved differences between trademark law, geographic indications and national trade-policy traditions.

Outcome

.WINE and .VIN were delegated in 2015.

2012–2013
Geographic identityLegal rightsGAC adviceFormal objection
The question

What happens when a trademark is also the name of a geographic region shared by more than one country?

FACT

Patagonia, Inc. applied for .PATAGONIA. Argentina raised a GAC Early Warning and the application faced Community Objections, including from Argentina’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Independent Objector. The application was withdrawn.

READING

Few cases explain the collision between brand identity and geographic identity more cleanly. The fact that a company owns a mark does not make every geographic meaning disappear.

Outcome

The .PATAGONIA application was withdrawn and the string was not delegated.

.islam · .halal
2012–2018
CommunityReligious sensitivityGovernment adviceAccountabilityGAC adviceFormal objectionAccountability reviewICANN Board decision
The question

Can a private applicant operate a globally sensitive religious term without broad support from the community it invokes?

FACT

Asia Green IT Systems applied for .ISLAM and .HALAL. GAC members raised sensitivities and concerns about community involvement and support, and the applications were held. The applicant later prevailed in an IRP on process issues, but after re-review the Board directed in 2018 that both applications not proceed.

READING

The case tests a hard question the DNS cannot solve technically: who, if anyone, can legitimately speak for a global religious community in a top-level namespace?

Outcome

.ISLAM and .HALAL did not proceed and were not delegated.

.merck · .emerck · .merckmsd

Legal rightsCompetitionAccountabilityFormal objectionCommunity Priority EvaluationAccountability review
The question

What do “trademark rights” mean when different companies legitimately use the same historic name in different markets?

FACT

Merck KGaA and Merck Registry Holdings pursued overlapping MERCK-related strings and filed objections against one another’s applications. The dispute moved through objection, community-priority and accountability mechanisms. A .MERCK TLD was finally delegated in 2026 to Merck Registry Holdings, Inc.

READING

The case breaks the comforting fiction that a famous brand name necessarily has one uncontested global owner. Domain governance has to operate across territorial trademark histories.

Outcome

.MERCK was delegated in April 2026 to Merck Registry Holdings, Inc.

.music
2012–2021
CommunityCompetitionCommunity Priority EvaluationFormal objectionICANN Board decision
The question

Who gets to define a global “music community” strongly enough to receive priority for .MUSIC?

FACT

Eight applicants sought .MUSIC. Competing applicants and music-industry organizations used objections and Community Priority Evaluation, followed by reconsideration activity. DotMusic Limited ultimately signed a community Registry Agreement in 2021 and .MUSIC was delegated later that year.

READING

The case shows that “community” is not a decorative label. In the new-gTLD process it can become a formal claim about representation, boundaries, support and enforceable registration policies.

Outcome

.MUSIC was delegated in 2021 to DotMusic Limited under a community Registry Agreement.

The strange Internet

Not just odd names. These are small fossils of what each era thought deserved its own piece of the Internet.
Strange Internet is now an editorial lens. Search and filtering live in the Explorer, where these records sit beside the rest of the namespace.
Strange Internet, round by round
FACTREADING

The unexpected is not unique to 2026. Compare curious applied-for strings, their outcomes and the limits of what the records prove across application rounds.

A namespace can be governed, but meaning also emerges from use.
A TLD has a formal status, but not necessarily a fixed cultural meaning. Registries define rules and eligibility; language, technology and communities can rewrite what people read after the dot. The same principle matters for .lugano: governance can define the perimeter, while actual use will shape what the namespace comes to mean.
FACTREADING

When the DNS remembers a different world

Country codes can outlive states, disappear with them, remain reserved, or describe places that barely behave like ordinary domain markets. The root is part directory, part institutional fossil record.

Ghosts of geopolitics

Some country-code domains survive political entities; others are deliberately retired after a transition.

.suActive legacy
FACT.SU was delegated in 1990 and IANA still marks it ACTIVE; IANA historical material identifies it as the Soviet Union code.
READINGA DNS label can outlive the state that originally gave it meaning.
Source 1 ↗Source 2 ↗
.yuRetired
FACT.YU was delegated for Yugoslavia in 1989 and removed from the root on 1 April 2010 after the transition to .RS and .ME.
READINGRetiring a ccTLD is a migration problem, not an instant edit to the map.
Source 1 ↗
.anRetired
FACT.AN represented the Netherlands Antilles. After the territory dissolved in 2010, the code lost eligibility and the domain was retired while successor namespaces were introduced.
READINGPolitical fragmentation can require several successor namespaces rather than a one-for-one rename.
Source 1 ↗Source 2 ↗
.tpRetired
FACT.TP represented Portuguese Timor. After Timor-Leste became independent, .TL replaced it and .TP was removed from the root in 2015.
READINGA ccTLD can become a legacy dependency that must be wound down years after the political transition.
Source 1 ↗Source 2 ↗

A reused code that was not redelegated

The history of a string and the history of the country code assigned to it can diverge.

.csRetired
FACT.CS was formerly delegated for Czechoslovakia and later retired. ISO reassigned CS to Serbia and Montenegro in 2003, but .CS was not redelegated for that country, which continued using .YU until .RS and .ME were created.
READINGReusing a country code does not automatically revive its former Internet delegation.
Source 1 ↗Source 2 ↗

A historical exception that stuck

The United Kingdom is one of the clearest reminders that DNS history predates today’s tidy eligibility rules.

.gb / .ukHistory
FACTISO uses GB, yet the operational British ccTLD is .UK. IANA lists .GB as a reserved domain and treats .UK as a grandfathered historical exception.
READINGInternet naming history sometimes wins over later standardisation.
Source 1 ↗Source 2 ↗Source 3 ↗

Namespaces with almost no market

A territory can qualify for a ccTLD even when ordinary public registrations are absent or the place itself has no conventional population.

.aqDelegated
FACT.AQ is the ccTLD for Antarctica and has been delegated since 1992.
READINGThe root can assign a geographic identity even to a continent without a normal nation-state or permanent population.
Source 1 ↗
.bvDelegated
FACT.BV belongs to Bouvet Island. Norid says the TLD has never been opened for domain registrations.
READINGA TLD can exist technically without becoming a public namespace market.
Source 1 ↗Source 2 ↗
.sjDelegated
FACT.SJ covers Svalbard and Jan Mayen. Norid says it has never been opened for registrations and points users toward .NO instead.
READINGEligibility for a ccTLD does not imply that second-level registrations must be offered.
Source 1 ↗Source 2 ↗

Beyond the nation-state — and beyond Latin script

The ccTLD system can represent a supranational entity and the same identity in multiple writing systems.

.euDelegated
FACT.EU is treated as a country-code TLD even though the European Union is not a state; IANA recognises EU through an exceptionally reserved eligibility path.
READINGThe country-code system contains institutional exceptions that do not map neatly onto sovereign states.
Source 1 ↗Source 2 ↗
.ею / .ευDelegated
FACTThe European Union also has Cyrillic .ею and Greek .ευ forms, delegated through the IDN ccTLD process.
READINGOne political identity can exist at the top level in several scripts while remaining part of the same global root.
Source 1 ↗Source 2 ↗
The root is not a clean map of today.
The DNS inherits geography from standards, but transitions take time and historical exceptions survive. That makes the root a record of political change, administrative convention and technical continuity — not merely a list of current countries.
How to read this section: an application or delegation is a FACT; counts derived from the published corpus are marked DERIVED; the cultural or technological meaning is a READING. A 2026 application is not yet a TLD.

Reveal Day is the first public snapshot, not the final string list

ICANN published the initial Reveal Day snapshot on 7 October. The Replacement Period is now open from 8 to 21 October; the confirmed string list and updated contention sets are scheduled for 17 November.

Applicants, primary strings, applicable variants/replacements, preliminary identical-string contention sets and public application data.

8–21 OCT · REPLACEMENT PERIOD

Eligible applicants may switch from their primary string to a replacement string.

17 NOV · STRING CONFIRMATION

Final applied-for string list and updated contention sets.

What Reveal Day already shows

The list is still provisional until 17 November, but several signals are already strong enough to describe without pretending that the round is finished.

2026 ANALYSIS

Demand is still geographically asymmetric

Of the 1,615 Reveal Day applications, 864 come from North America and 506 from Europe, compared with 218 from Asia-Pacific, 16 from Africa and 11 from Latin America and the Caribbean. This is application geography, not Internet-user geography.

2026 ANALYSIS

The round is also a portfolio game

ICANN reports 333 .Brand applications. A secondary analysis of the public application records also shows several registry specialists filing dozens or more applications, so the round is not simply 481 organizations making one bet each.

2026 ANALYSIS

AI and agents are the new vocabulary

In the public APS corpus for Reveal Day, 7 October 2026, .agent has 13 applications, .api 10, .robot 9 and .agi 7. OpenAI appears with .openai and .chatgpt. These cases show AI and automation vocabulary in the 2026 applications. They do not, by themselves, measure an overall shift relative to 2012.

2026 ANALYSIS

Scarcity did not disappear

Reveal Day produced 263 preliminary identical-string contention sets involving 891 application records. Replacement strings can remove or create pressure, while later singular/plural, string-confusion and similarity processes can still alter contention.

The public APS follows its own publication schedule

ICANN states on APS About that the public website is not updated between Reveal Day and String Confirmation Day. Later updates are regular, but are not made in real time; applicants must consult TAMS for the most up-to-date information about their own applications. The replacement-choice window closes on 21 October 2026 at 23:59 UTC. Publication of the confirmed strings and updated contention sets is scheduled for 17 November 2026.

An unchanged public page during this interval is therefore not evidence that no internal processing has occurred. On 18 October the .wdo page still displays an administrative check. The public schedule neither establishes the outcome of that check nor promises that it will be resolved on 17 November.

A process observed as it unfolds

Timeline

The 2026 New gTLD Program is not just a historical dataset. We can follow its decisive public events as they happen, with the .lugano application providing an unusually direct vantage point. This is a chronicle of milestones, not an application manual.

What the rules say

The official ICANN program defines milestones, conditions and possible outcomes. Its documents are the source for dates and procedural claims.

What the round reveals

Reveal Day and later decisions show the global field: competing ideas, shared strings, objections, evaluations and changing expectations.

What .lugano lets us observe

A real candidacy gives the research a participant's perspective, but only verifiable and publishable events enter this public record.

CASE 01 · REVEAL DAY 2026

One application missing. Two different questions.

The figures differed by just one, yet the distinction matters. A paid-application count, an official Reveal Day total and a frozen secondary index do not describe exactly the same publication state.

Partly explained · one question remains open
1,616ICANN, 22 September · paid applications proceeding
1,615ICANN, 7 October · official Reveal Day applications
1,614Secondary snapshot of 7 October · observed on 8 October

The 1,614 figure comes from the frozen nTLDData-based index (480 applicants), not an ICANN-published application-level export.

The Explorer’s 2026 layer represents 1,608 applications associated with primary strings (980 distinct primary strings), plus six variant-only applications for existing TLDs. Its 1,614 indexed applications are therefore neither 1,614 new strings nor the complete set of 1,615 applications reported by ICANN.

Documented omission 1,615 → 1,614

The .wdo application: a documented absence from the public list

ICANN's APS Applications page explicitly says that application WDO2627T-T45217 for .wdo (World Data Organization, China) is still undergoing an administrative check and is therefore absent from the public applications list. The application detail page independently confirms that status. This gives a documented explanation for why the visible list can contain one fewer application than the official aggregate. The independent secondary snapshot is consistent with that omission; its coverage is not being certified as a complete APS export.

Cause not established 1,616 → 1,615

Why did the official count fall before Reveal Day?

On 22 September ICANN reported 1,616 paid applications proceeding. On 7 October the official Reveal Day total was 1,615. The verified public sources reviewed here do not identify which record accounts for the change or why. Withdrawal, administrative rejection, a payment issue or a timing adjustment would be speculation. This question remains open.

The regional discrepancy: a second check

Only Asia-Pacific differs between the official Reveal Day application counts and the project's preserved secondary index. The applicant count also differs by one in precisely that region.

Region ICANN Index Gap
North America864864—
Europe506506—
Asia-Pacific218217+1
Africa1616—
Latin America & Caribbean1111—
Total1,6151,614+1

Across five regions, official totals add to 1,615 applications from 481 applicants; the secondary index has 1,614 from 480. The .wdo applicant is in China. The regional match supports the APS footnote but does not replace a one-to-one reconciliation of all application IDs.

An independent researcher's CSV check

On 8 October, Stéphane Bortzmeyer examined the public CSV: 2,783 total rows, 1,614 applications when replacement-string rows are removed, and 480 applicants. Exported rows, applications and requested strings are not interchangeable because one application can yield several rows. The independent check corroborates the visible shortfall but does not explain the earlier change in the official total.

A widely reported explanation is not a complete reconciliation

CircleID placed the .wdo administrative check alongside the change from 1,616 to 1,615. In its 8 October notice JPNIC similarly described 1,616 paid applications, 1,615 published and one under administrative check. Yet APS already reports 1,615 active in its statistics while the independent public index identifies 1,614. These accounts are relevant interpretations, not an ID-by-ID reconciliation proving which application caused the earlier official decrease.

Why should anyone care about a difference of one?

Because a statistic, an application record and a publishable application list are different objects. The exercise shows why researchers must capture the date, scope and source of a number before comparing it, and why public visibility should never be confused with acceptance, approval or eventual delegation.

Evidence, not speculation

The 1,616 and 1,615 totals are direct ICANN statements; 1,614 is a time-stamped secondary index preserved by this project. The APS footnote documents .wdo's omission, but does not explain the earlier change in ICANN totals. The two gaps are therefore tracked separately. This episode is a corrigible editorial observation, not a revision of the archived RR1 dataset.

What would close the remaining question?

A dated ICANN explanation connecting the September and October totals, a change to the .wdo administrative-check record, or a public list that can be reconciled application by application. Any substantive correction will be dated, sourced and documented in the project history.

Review of 18 October 2026

A separate count question now has a record-level answer

The archived official APS export contains 1,614 base applications, including six for variants of existing TLDs. Excluding those six yields 1,608 applications and 980 distinct primary strings, exactly the same set of names as in the frozen secondary inventory. Including them yields 986 primary strings. Field Note 04 lists the six IDs and the reproducible filter. This finding does not resolve the earlier 1,616 → 1,615 discrepancy.

Sanctions & the DNS: what ICANN can and cannot do ↗

CASE 02 · NAMES AND PRIOR RIGHTS

Two organizations, one acronym: who may seek .wdo?

The .wdo applicant is the World Data Organization, launched in Beijing in 2026. But the World Design Organization dates back to 1957, uses WDO and holds a registered trademark. Is there already a legal dispute? Public evidence does not establish one.

Shared acronym documented · No verified dispute
World Data OrganizationBeijing · established 2026 · .wdo applicant
World Design OrganizationMontréal · founded 1957 · wdo.org

First distinction: they are not the same organization

ICANN names World Data Organization, located in China, as the applicant for .wdo under WDO2627T-T45217, still undergoing an administrative check. World Design Organization is a separate Montréal-based body involved in industrial design and using wdo.org. Sharing the initials WDO proves no corporate or institutional connection between them.

Two histories, almost seventy years apart

World Data Organization was launched in Beijing on 30 March 2026; the Chinese Academy of Sciences reports that Tan Tieniu was elected council chair. World Design Organization was founded in 1957 as Icsid and adopted its current name in 2015. The application therefore concerns initials with an established public history, but that history alone cannot determine entitlement to the TLD.

A verifiable earlier right is not an automatic veto

Canada's CIPO registry records the word mark WORLD DESIGN ORGANIZATION (WDO), filed on 23 October 2015 and registered as TMA1008130 on 2 November 2018, with active registration. Trademark protection has a defined scope: it does not automatically confer ownership of the .wdo top-level domain, nor prove that the organization has filed an objection.

What does the ICANN procedure allow?

The 2026 Applicant Guidebook permits a Legal Rights Objection by a party with standing claiming infringement of existing rights, backed by evidence. ICANN announced a public-input and objections window running from 17 November 2026 to 16 March 2027. Possible standing is a starting point, not an adjudicated claim. As of 10 October, no objection from World Design Organization concerning .wdo has been verified.

Compliance context, not an explanation for the check

Another documented fact concerns Tan Tieniu: the Chinese Academy of Sciences identifies him as a World Data Organization leader, while a 17 July 2026 US OFAC update lists him under Hong Kong Autonomy Act measures on the Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions List. That entry concerns an individual, not proof that World Data Organization is itself designated. No ICANN source connects it to the administrative check of .wdo; a causal claim would be speculation.

What remains unknown

ICANN has not published the reason for the administrative check on WDO2627T-T45217. There is no verified objection by World Design Organization, refusal, established infringement, or decision on the merits of the application. Neither the new organization's age, another body's trademark nor a leader's sanctions record can be used to infer the cause.

How this case will be followed

A revision will require new primary evidence: an APS status change, published comments or objections involving .wdo, official statements by either WDO, a decision affecting the name, or a relevant OFAC change. Each change will be dated and sourced. Research must not invent a dispute before one exists.

CITIES, RULES AND OUTCOMES

Turning a digital commons into verifiable choices

The .lugano case follows a project in formation. Official sources describe its intentions; the examples and operational criteria below are the author's analysis, not live services or adopted rules.

What is documented

The City is the applicant and describes a staged opening with a substantial, verifiable territorial connection. Final criteria are not yet settled. The municipal FAQ says private sponsors cover the application fee, with no charge to city finances; that does not make future operating costs zero. lugano.ch remains the institutional website and MyLugano keeps its role.

Analytical proposal, not adopted policy

Who gets a name that represents a whole community?

Hypothetical examples, not allocations: cultura.lugano, ristoranti.lugano, quartieri.lugano. A collective name could be reserved, run as a shared gateway or allocated with explicit obligations, duration and transparent criteria. The proposal is to make eligibility, institutional-name protection, dispute handling and allocation review understandable, within ICANN rules and applicable law.

Editorial review: 17 October 2026

Reasons and precedents
FACTREADING

Why would a city seek its own top-level domain?

The interesting question is not whether a city can place its name after a dot. It is what public value, safeguards and services could justify operating a distinct namespace. These are criteria for evaluation, not promises already fulfilled.

A name people can recognise

A .lugano address could signal a connection with the city, but the suffix alone would not certify its owner. Any trustworthy use would require clear eligibility, verification and anti-impersonation rules.

Public-interest governance

A civic namespace raises choices about reserved names, fair allocation, security, abuse handling and review of disputed decisions. These choices must be made transparent if the application succeeds; a domain extension does not settle them automatically.

An address, not an identity certificate

The DNS translates names into technical destinations. It does not, by itself, prove that a service is official or trustworthy. Verification, accessible public registers and clear responsibility could add that layer.

Build in stages, if approved

A possible sequence starts with a secure registry and transparent registration policy, then adds verified services and interoperable public-interest components. None of these stages is operational merely because the application is public.

FACTREADING

What Swiss precedents can and cannot tell us

Geographic and place-linked TLDs already exist. They help frame questions about eligibility, operation and public identity, but they do not predetermine the governance or the outcome of the .lugano application.

Cities and territories have taken different paths

Cases such as .berlin, .nyc and .zuerich show that geographic names can enter the DNS under different operators and registration policies. A shared geographic label does not mean a shared governance model.

Explore geographic TLDs

.zuerich: a Swiss point of reference

The existing .zuerich Registry Agreement is a useful primary source for examining a Swiss geographic TLD. It is a precedent, not evidence that .lugano has been delegated or would use identical rules.

ICANN · .zuerich ↗
Distinctive value, not an invented first
Because .zuerich already exists, .lugano should not be presented as Switzerland's first geographic TLD. Its potential originality lies in the proposed public-interest use of naming, trust and digital commons, which would still need to be built and assessed.

Uses and criteria for results

CITIES, RULES AND OUTCOMES

Recognisable to people, verifiable by machines

Analytical proposal, not adopted policy

The suffix alone certifies neither identity, quality nor authority. DNSSEC authenticates DNS data origin and integrity, not a registrant's commercial trustworthiness. For services and software agents, our proposal distinguishes who the entity is, which service it represents and which operations it may perform. Identification, verifiable service descriptions and limited, revocable authorisation need additional components.

A business admitted to .lugano does not become an official municipal service. Verified territorial membership must remain distinguishable from institutional representation, including for first-time visitors.

IETF · RFC 4033, sections 3–4 ↗

Editorial review: 17 October 2026

CITIES, RULES AND OUTCOMES

Open in response to usefulness, not just a calendar

Analytical proposal, not adopted policy

1 · Recognisable early uses

Before scaling adoption, test a few useful services, clear responsibilities, support and user understanding.

2 · Broader local participation

Involve local organisations and registrars, explain criteria and prices, and measure actual use rather than name requests alone.

3 · Interoperable services

Trial additional functions only with verified identities, permissions, revocation and oversight. These are possibilities, not existing capabilities.

Before opening, test websites, email, forms, authentication and integrations: ICANN warns that delegation does not guarantee immediate software acceptance. Registrar distribution also needs to be built; it is not automatic.

geoTLD.group · Local by Design (27.07.2026) ↗ICANN · Applicant Guidebook, 2.3 / 2.10 ↗

Decisions still to be made

Who qualifies, which names are reserved, what prices and protections apply, how costs are funded and how outcomes are evaluated all need published answers when settled. We state no firm launch date and do not treat commercial expressions of interest as guaranteed reservations.

Scenarios and proposed path
VISION · IF DELEGATEDNOT YET IMPLEMENTED

.lugano — from a name to a trust layer

A vision for what the namespace could become if the application succeeds. This is direction, not an announcement of services already implemented.
The ambition is not simply to put Lugano after a dot. It is to create a public-interest namespace in which trust can become visible, governable and eventually machine-readable.
01VISION

Public stewardship

Public responsibilities, access criteria and review procedures should be identifiable in the published rules.

02VISION

Qualified participation

Different classes of users or services could carry explicit eligibility and accountability rules.

03VISION

Security & interoperability

Minimum technical requirements and open interfaces can make trust operational rather than merely symbolic.

04VISION

Machine-readable trust

In the longer term, software and AI agents could verify who they are interacting with, what a service is allowed to do and which rules apply.

VISION

An illustrative progression

Each step would require its own governance, legal and technical decisions after a successful ICANN process.
01
VISION
Secure registry foundation

Registry policies, reserved names, institutional domains, abuse handling and operational continuity.

02
VISION
Verified ecosystem

Qualified organizations, services and local actors with clear conditions of use and transparent responsibilities.

03
VISION
Digital commons layer

Shared technical components, metadata and interoperable services that reduce friction for the local ecosystem.

04
VISION
Agent-ready trust

Machine-readable identity, delegation and service discovery so intelligent systems can evaluate trust as well as humans do.

FACTNothing in this section implies that ICANN has assigned .lugano or that these services already exist. It describes a possible design direction, subject to the application outcome and future decisions by the City.

Risks and next checks

READING

A vision to test against public evidence

These are editorial questions for assessing a possible civic namespace. They describe neither adopted municipal targets nor services already delivered.

A clear use

Which task would become easier or more reliable for a person, organization or service? A distinctive suffix alone does not demonstrate that benefit.

Actual adoption

Do names lead to services people use? Published examples of active use would be stronger evidence than the number of names reserved or announced.

Rules that can be checked

Can users understand who is eligible, who is responsible and how a problem can be reported? Confidence should rest on published rules and accountable practice.

Working connections

Can people and software use the services through documented interfaces and accepted standards? Public documentation and working demonstrations would make this claim testable.

Questions raised by the data

How the language of TLD applications mirrors the society of each era.
From .berlin to .lugano: how cities entered the DNS root.
What disputed strings reveal about trademarks, geography, communities, governments and ICANN accountability.
What the 2026 contention sets reveal about AI, agents, finance, brands and identity.
Can a city TLD evolve from digital branding into trust infrastructure?
How country codes, renewals, auctions, acquisitions and application fees turn naming infrastructure into economic value.
When does a TLD become a marker of language, locality, identity or belonging rather than simply an address?

The author’s position

Robert Bregy is the municipal secretary of the City of Lugano and is involved in the .lugano project. This publication is a personal, independent research project. Its interpretations and scenarios do not constitute an official City position or decision.

READING

What makes a TLD successful?

Registration volume is only one metric. A brand TLD, a verified community namespace and a civic TLD may have completely different purposes, so success has to be measured against mission.

01

Scale

How many names are registered, and how quickly the namespace grows or contracts.

02

Active use

Whether names resolve to real services, websites, email or machine-readable endpoints.

03

Renewal

Whether registrants keep names over time rather than treating the namespace as disposable inventory.

04

Trust and abuse

Security controls, abuse rates, verification requirements and credibility attached to the namespace.

05

Diversity

How registrations are distributed across registrants, registrars, sectors and geographies.

06

Purpose fulfilment

Whether the namespace achieves the mission for which it exists, even with modest raw volume.

07

Public value

For civic namespaces: local adoption, verified actors, useful services, interoperability and measurable public value.

This is a framework, not a ranking. A TLD should be judged against the job it is meant to do.

How to read this publication

FACT marks information supported by a cited source. READING marks an interpretation of data, history or institutional significance. VISION marks a proposed future direction. Systematic life-history evidence and editorially selected governance cases are kept distinct.

FACTREADINGVISION

Methodological guardrails

  • “Geographic” is an ICANN application classification; “city TLD” is a narrower analytical classification used in this publication.
  • Application counts, unique-string counts, registry portfolios, RSP-managed TLDs and delegated-TLD counts are different metrics and are never blended.
  • The 2026 application layer is post-Reveal. Official aggregate metrics and preliminary contention data are preserved locally. The Explorer integrates a locally frozen secondary snapshot of the Reveal Day primary-string inventory; a complete local APS corpus at individual-application level is not claimed. Strings and contention sets may still change during the Replacement Period before String Confirmation Day.
  • “Zeitgeist” themes and the five-layer power model are analytical classifications and remain separate from official ICANN fields.
  • Economic metrics retain their original accounting basis and currency. Public revenue, company revenue, operating income, transaction value, auction price and application fees are never treated as one comparable measure.
  • Social significance is not inferred from registration volume. Registry charters, eligibility rules and documented community policies are FACT; the broader meaning assigned to them in this publication is a READING.

Internet architecture · Governance explainer

Who controls access to the Internet?

A website can exist in the global DNS and still be unreachable from one network or country. Follow a request to see where control may be exercised, and why ICANN is not the Internet's universal censorship authority.

The distinction

DNS names, TLDs, registry contracts, national network filters and platform content decisions are separate layers. They can affect the same website, but they operate differently.

Try the access-control simulator

Choose one hypothetical intervention. The diagram shows which stage fails and whether the name may still exist outside the affected network. This is an explanatory model, not a real connectivity test.

Example addresshttps://www.example.com/

Choose a scenario

Before the visit: the name must exist

The registry and registrar manage the domain's registration and authoritative DNS status. They are not contacted as an extra network hop every time someone opens a website.

  • passed

    TLD, registry & registration

    Is the domain registered and delegated? This is an upstream lifecycle condition, not a packet filter.

During the visit: the user's actual request path

  1. passed

    DNS resolver

    Can the user's resolver translate the hostname into a usable IP address?

  2. passed

    ISP, routing & IP access

    Can packets travel from this network to the destination?

  3. passed

    TLS handshake & traffic filters

    Can the encrypted connection be established? Some metadata may be visible.

  4. passed

    Hosting, application & content

    Does the remote service answer and provide the requested resource?

Available in this scenario

The request completes

The name resolves, packets are routed, TLS succeeds and the service responds. This is a simplified reference case.

What happens to the global name?The domain remains present in the DNS.
What can users reach?The example service is reachable.
Who might enforce this?No intervention is simulated.
[1]
Access interrupted in this scenario

The resolver changes the answer

A local resolver may refuse the lookup or return a blocking address. Authoritative DNS and the TLD can still work normally elsewhere. An alternate resolver only helps if this is the sole relevant restriction.

What happens to the global name?The name may still be globally delegated.
What can users reach?Users of the affected resolver may not reach the target by its name.
Who might enforce this?A network operator, sometimes under a legal order.
[1][8]
Access interrupted in this scenario

The DNS name works. The route does not.

Even a valid DNS answer is insufficient when a network blocks access to the destination IP address or relevant route. A shared IP can host unrelated sites, creating collateral effects.

What happens to the global name?The name and DNS answer may be intact.
What can users reach?Connections to the blocked destination fail on that network.
Who might enforce this?An ISP or another network operator.
[1]
Access interrupted in this scenario

The secure connection fails

A filter can interrupt a connection during the TLS handshake, for example using visible server-name metadata when present. DNS can be correct and the server operational. Encryption details and countermeasures evolve.

What happens to the global name?The domain can remain normally resolved.
What can users reach?The HTTPS connection may reset or time out.
Who might enforce this?Network filtering equipment operated by providers or intermediaries.
[1][6]
Access interrupted in this scenario

The server or platform refuses the content

An application can remove a page, restrict an account, or geo-block content. The DNS and network can still function perfectly; this is not an ICANN action.

What happens to the global name?The domain can remain registered and resolved.
What can users reach?The requested service or content is unavailable under the platform's rules.
Who might enforce this?Hosting providers, applications or platform operators.
[1]
Access interrupted in this scenario

The domain's registration or delegation changes

Registry or registrar procedures may suspend a domain. Depending on the action, authoritative DNS may no longer publish the same delegation. This is not equivalent to deleting the entire TLD.

What happens to the global name?This individual registration/delegation may cease working globally.
What can users reach?Reachability may be affected across many networks.
Who might enforce this?Registries and registrars within applicable procedures and contracts.
[4]
Access interrupted in this scenario

Connectivity is cut for a population

A shutdown interrupts Internet communications for a region or group. It is not a DNS or TLD deletion. Its scope can differ between mobile and fixed networks and need not be technically total.

What happens to the global name?Global DNS names are not necessarily changed.
What can users reach?Broad groups of services become unavailable from the affected network.
Who might enforce this?Network operators, potentially acting under government orders.
[2][3]

The registry step describes control over registration and authoritative delegation, not an additional network hop on each visit. The exact outcome depends on how the measure is implemented.

Who controls what?

The same incident can involve a legal decision, a network-level enforcement action and an unrelated global DNS state. Do not confuse the actor with the technical layer.

ICANN / IANA

Coordinate names and the root-zone framework; they do not generally order national ISPs to block websites. The 2022 Ukraine letter illustrates the limits of this mandate.

[4]

Registry / registrar

Govern registrations and contractual suspensions under the rules that apply to a TLD. Actions affecting a registration are not the same as country-level filtering.

[4]

Government / authority

May create legal obligations within its jurisdiction. The scope, safeguards and justification depend on the law and on the measure.

[8][9]

Access provider

May implement DNS, IP, traffic or routing restrictions; different networks in the same country can behave differently.

[1][8]

Platform / hosting

May moderate content, refuse service or apply territorial restrictions without changing DNS delegation.

[1]

Five documented examples, five different contexts

A curated historical selection with dated evidence, not a complete or current inventory of countries that restrict online access.

2023

China · DNS injection plus TLS interference

OONI documented that access to its own website was disrupted in China by injected DNS answers and interference during TLS connections. This observation concerns the tested services and networks, not an assertion about every website in China.

OONI study published 2023

[5]
2023–2024

Russia · DNS and traffic-level filtering

In measurements from September 2023 to September 2024, OONI and RKS Global documented blocking of independent media. TLS handshake interference predominated in the studied sample, alongside some DNS-based blocks.

OONI / RKS Global, December 2024

[6]
June 2025

Iran · suspected app blocking and connectivity disruption

Between 15 June and 12 July 2025, OONI observed repeated anomalies consistent with possible WhatsApp blocking on some Iranian networks, without establishing that it affected every network. During the June conflict, OONI and other monitoring systems recorded evidence of severe connectivity disruption. App-level interference and a network shutdown remain distinct findings.

OONI findings, June–July 2025

[7][3]
2026

Switzerland · legally mandated DNS blocking

Gespa and the Federal Gaming Board maintain lists of unlicensed foreign gambling offers. Swiss access providers must apply DNS blocks for the listed domains. The measure is domestic; it does not remove those TLDs from the global root.

Gespa official blocklist, August 2026

[8]
2017

Catalonia (Spain) · domain actions and network blocking

During the 2017 referendum, OONI measured DNS tampering and HTTP blocking of referendum sites. Some .cat domains were also redirected at the DNS level after Fundació .cat implemented a court order, while ISPs applied other blocks. Actions affecting particular registrations are not removal of the .cat TLD: it is a sponsored gTLD, not a ccTLD.

OONI measurements, September–October 2017

[9]

Measurements are evidence, not an automatic verdict

OONI distinguishes automatically confirmed blocks (for example known block pages or known DNS censorship addresses) from anomalies that can have benign causes. Repeated results on identified networks and dates strengthen an interpretation; one failure cannot prove censorship. Internet Society Pulse separately records documented connectivity disruptions under its own inclusion methodology. Neither dataset is a universal real-time score for all countries.

[1][3]

Source identifiers accompany the case studies and mechanisms. These are original institutional or measurement-project records, not generalized country rankings.

Governance explainer · OFAC & DNS

When a global Internet meets national sanctions

ICANN coordinates a global naming system, yet must obey the laws that apply to it. That creates constraints on who can obtain a new gTLD, but does not give ICANN a general power to disconnect countries from the DNS.

Legal compliance

ICANN may be barred from providing services to certain applicants unless an authorization or exemption applies.

Technical neutrality

ICANN says its mandate is not to impose geopolitical sanctions or unilaterally disconnect country-code domains.

What the rules actually mean

Why US sanctions reach a global organization

ICANN is a California-based nonprofit. Its global mission does not exempt it from applicable US laws, including OFAC economic and trade sanctions. These laws govern certain dealings with people, entities and jurisdictions. They do not make every domain associated with a sanctioned country illegal.

[2][5]

New gTLD applications: designated persons are not the same as residents

For the 2026 round, ICANN explicitly says it cannot accept applications from individuals or entities on OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. A separate question arises when an applicant is not listed but is located in a sanctioned jurisdiction: whether an exemption or US authorization permits ICANN to provide services. Neither nationality alone nor an individual's listing proves that a different organization is sanctioned.

[1][2]

Licenses matter. Approval is not automatic.

OFAC distinguishes general licenses, which authorize classes of transactions under stated conditions, from specific licenses granted case by case. ICANN says it has previously obtained licenses for applicants in sanctioned countries who were not individually designated. ICANN has no duty to apply in every case and OFAC is not obliged to grant a request. ICANN's community has also recommended examining general licenses to reduce recurring barriers.

[2][3][4][9]

Four different layers, four different consequences

An applicant for a new gTLD, a TLD registry operator, an accredited registrar and a customer registering a second-level domain are not interchangeable roles. Contracting, accreditation, sales and DNS delegation trigger different obligations and involve different actors. A blocked transaction with one actor does not automatically erase a ccTLD from the root zone or revoke every name registered under it.

[2][8]

Even 'sanctioned country' does not mean 'no domain names'

A concrete counterexample: OFAC's Cuba guidance says domain-name registration is among the Internet-communications services authorized in most circumstances under a relevant general license. This is not a universal exemption. It shows why the exact sanctions program, transaction, parties and authorization matter more than a country label.

[6][4]

OFAC is not the only sanctions framework

UN, EU, UK and national rules may also matter to actors within their respective jurisdiction or where legally applicable. Their scopes differ. ICANN's US obligations should not be conflated with a universal rule binding every non-US registrar or domain holder in precisely the same way.

[2][5]

What the 2026 evidence does not establish

ICANN reported 1,616 paid applications on 22 September and 1,615 at Reveal Day on 7 October. It has not publicly identified an OFAC exclusion as the reason for the change. The .wdo application has been subject to a separately documented administrative check, but its precise reason is not publicly established. Treat sanctions as relevant background, not a proposed explanation for either observation.

[10][11][12]

Four documented moments

These events belong to different legal and procedural categories. They are not four examples of OFAC removing TLDs.

2012

No sanctions-based rejections reported

ICANN states that no application in the 2012 new gTLD round was rejected because of its sanctions-compliance obligations. This does not mean that sanctions screening or licensing was absent.

[3]
2014

A court refused attachment of .ir, .sy and .kp

Judgment creditors sought to seize country-code TLDs associated with Iran, Syria and North Korea. A US federal court quashed the attempt. This was a civil enforcement dispute about attachable property, not ICANN rejecting a new gTLD application under OFAC rules.

[7]
2022

ICANN declined to disconnect Russian ccTLDs

Following Ukraine's request concerning .ru, .рф and .su, ICANN said its technical mandate did not extend to imposing sanctions or unilaterally cutting off national domains. It also noted that ICANN does not issue SSL certificates or control all root-server nodes.

[8]
2026

Eligibility and legal screening are explicit

The new Applicant Guidebook and associated FAQs make sanctions compliance part of the 2026 process and differentiate SDN-listed applicants from potentially licensable transactions involving other applicants.

[1][2]

Why this matters for the 2026 round

The difference between 1,616 paid applications announced on 22 September and the 1,615 reported at Reveal Day is a documented discrepancy, not proof of sanctions enforcement. The public administrative check involving .wdo also has no confirmed OFAC cause. Follow the two investigations separately.

Field Note · The Reveal Day numbers ↗ Field Note · Two WDOs and .wdo ↗

How domestic Internet blocking differs

OFAC sanctions constrain certain legal transactions involving ICANN. A country or network can also restrict users' access at DNS, IP or TLS level, even when the top-level domain remains globally valid.
